children.title: Dual Strict-Convexity Regime
children.top_down_role: Strict-convexity behavior on the conjugate side of the correspondence.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is essentially smooth if and only if \(f^*\) is essentially strictly convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical finite-dimensional essential-smoothness and essential-strict-convexity conjugacy
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional essential regularity duality, avoiding an unjustified global strict-convexity claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is essentially smooth—differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), with \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to+\infty\) whenever interior points \(x_k\) approach a boundary point—if and only if \(f^*\) is essentially strictly convex. Here essential strict convexity means strict convexity on every convex subset of \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*\), together with local boundedness of \((\partial f^*)^{-1}\) on its domain. Conjugation exchanges these two regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential smoothness of a closed convex function is dual to essential strict convexity of its conjugate, on the subdifferential-reachable domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Strict-Convexity Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The essential-smoothness/essential-strict-convexity duality fits the leaf, but the exact theorem and the stated characterization of essential strict convexity require an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Regularity Reciprocity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting smoothness-to-strict-convexity reciprocity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smooth strict convexity alone does not imply a globally strongly convex or everywhere differentiable conjugate.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the exponential function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary separating qualitative smoothness from quantitative conjugate regularity.

source_refs.locator: 5 Smoothness and Strong Convexity p. 107
source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Although \(f(x)=e^x\) is smooth and strictly convex on \(\mathbb{R}\), its gradient is not globally Lipschitz. Its conjugate is
\[
f^*(u)=
\begin{cases}
u\log u-u,&u>0,\\
0,&u=0,\\
+\infty,&u<0.
\end{cases}
\]
On \((0,+\infty)\), one has \((f^*)''(u)=1/u\), whose infimum is zero; hence \(f^*\) is not globally strongly convex. Moreover, \(f^*\) has no finite derivative at the boundary point \(u=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential is smooth and strictly convex, but its conjugate is neither globally strongly convex nor differentiable at the boundary of its domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Reciprocity Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator, Support, Gauge, Polar, and Subdifferential Dictionary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. When gauges are used, additionally assume \(0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex set–function correspondences organized for subgradient calculations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The associated functions and sets are \[\iota_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C,\end{cases}\quad \sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle=\iota_C^*(u),\] \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\geq0:x\in tC\},\qquad C^\circ=\{u:\langle u,x\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}.\] Their subdifferential dictionary includes \[\partial\iota_C(x)=N_C(x),\qquad \partial\sigma_C(u)=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\},\] with the latter set empty when the support supremum is not attained. If \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains zero, then \[\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad \gamma_C^*=\iota_{C^\circ}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set can be represented by its indicator, support function, gauge, or polar. The indicator's subdifferential is the normal cone. The support function's subdifferential is the maximizing exposed face. For a closed convex set containing zero, its gauge is the support function of the polar, so gauge subgradients are supporting points of the polar.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\partial\sigma_C(u)\iff u\in N_C(x)\iff \langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u).\]
For finite \(\gamma_C(x)\), \[u\in\partial\gamma_C(x)\iff u\in C^\circ\text{ and }\langle u,x\rangle=\gamma_C(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is the unit ball of a norm, \(\gamma_C\) is that norm and \(C^\circ\) is its dual unit ball.
If \(C\) is a cone, its gauge is an indicator-like function and set polarity reduces to cone polarity.
immediate_consequences_latex: Normal and exposed-face relations are inverse through the pairing \(x\leftrightarrow u\).
Set constraints and support maximization can be treated with ordinary Fenchel subgradients.
boundary_notes: For nonclosed or nonconvex \(C\), support and polar operations retain only the closed convex hull together with the origin where appropriate.
A gauge may be extended-valued when \(C\) is not absorbing.

children.title: Indicator–Normal-Cone Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between extended-valued constraint models and convex-set normal geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Indicator Subdifferential as a Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Define its extended-valued indicator \(\iota_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-analytic normal cone; no smoothness or closedness is needed for the pointwise identity, although closedness is standard in applications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The indicator and convex normal cone are \[\iota_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C,\end{cases}\qquad N_C(x)=\begin{cases}\{u:\langle u,z-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in C\},&x\in C,\\\varnothing,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] Their canonical correspondence is the identity \[\partial\iota_C(x)=N_C(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] Thus a normal vector is exactly a subgradient of the extended-valued constraint function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator is zero on the feasible set and infinite outside it. Its subgradient inequality at a feasible point becomes the defining normal inequality against every point of the set. Outside the set, both the indicator subdifferential and the normal cone are empty.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x\in C\), \[u\in\partial\iota_C(x)\iff \sup_{z\in C}\langle u,z-x\rangle\leq0.\]
For \(x\in C\), \[u\in N_C(x)\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle u,z\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\) and \(C\) is full-dimensional, then \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\).
For a closed affine subspace \(C=x_0+V\), \(N_C(x)=V^\perp\) at every \(x\in C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The constrained stationarity condition for minimizing \(f\) over \(C\) can be written \(0\in\partial(f+\iota_C)(x)\).
Normal-cone calculus is a special case of subdifferential calculus for extended-valued functions.
boundary_notes: This is the convex normal cone; limiting, proximal, and Clarke normal cones are different objects for nonconvex sets.
At infeasible points \(x\notin C\), the value is empty rather than a cone containing zero.

notation.meaning: Normal cone to C at x

source_refs.locator: 6.4 Tangent and Normal Cones p. 125

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\delta_C(x)=
\begin{cases}
0,&x\in C,\\
+\infty,&x\notin C.
\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
\inf_{x\in C}g(x)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(g(x)+\delta_C(x)\bigr).
\]
Moreover, \(\partial\delta_C(x)=N_C(x)=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,z-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }z\in C\}\) when \(x\in C\), while both sets are empty when \(x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the convex indicator of C encodes the constraint x in C, and the indicator's subdifferential is the normal cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Encoding by Indicators

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-Valued Encoding of a Convex Constraint
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty. For convex optimization, assume both \(f\) and \(C\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value and solution-set encoding; subdifferential stationarity additionally uses convexity and an applicable sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the indicator \(\iota_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise, and the unconstrained extended-valued objective \[F(x)=f(x)+\iota_C(x).\] Then \[\operatorname{dom}F=\operatorname{dom}f\cap C,\qquad \inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}F(x)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x),\] and \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}F(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x).\] When \(f\) is proper convex, \(C\) is convex, and a qualification such as \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing\) holds, \[\partial F(x)=\partial f(x)+N_C(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the indicator of \(C\) makes every infeasible point have infinite objective value while leaving feasible objective values unchanged. Therefore the constrained and extended-valued unconstrained problems have identical infima and minimizers. Under the standard convex sum-rule qualification, stationarity becomes a balance between an objective subgradient and a normal vector.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C}f\iff 0\in\partial(f+\iota_C)(x)\] whenever the convex minimum is attained and the subdifferential criterion applies.
Under the sum-rule qualification, \[0\in\partial f(x)+N_C(x)\] is the encoded first-order optimality relation.
special_cases_latex: For \(f\equiv0\), every point of \(C\) minimizes \(\iota_C\).
If \(C=\{x:Ax=b\}\), the normal term lies in \(\operatorname{ran}A^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Feasibility is represented by finiteness of the extended-valued objective.
Multiple convex constraints can be encoded by the indicator of their intersection.
boundary_notes: If \(C=\varnothing\), the encoded objective is identically \(+\infty\) and is not proper.
The equality \(\partial(f+\iota_C)=\partial f+N_C\) can fail without a qualification condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
One has \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\). If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), then
\[
N_C(x)=\operatorname{lin}(C-C)^\perp;
\]
in particular, \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\) at an interior point of a full-dimensional set. At a boundary point of a full-dimensional closed convex set, \(N_C(x)\) contains a nonzero vector. If \(F\) is a face of \(C\), then \(N_C(x)\) is constant for \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal cones are tangent-cone polars: trivial in full-dimensional interiors, orthogonal to lower-dimensional affine hulls, nontrivial at boundaries, and constant on face interiors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Cone Regimes at Exterior, Interior, Boundary, and Relative-Interior Points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(V=\operatorname{par}C=\operatorname{aff}C-\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex geometry, including lower-dimensional sets through relative interior and the parallel subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[N_C(x)=\begin{cases}\{u:\langle u,z-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in C\},&x\in C,\\\varnothing,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] Position determines the basic regimes. If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), then \[N_C(x)=V^\perp.\] Hence, if \(C\) is full-dimensional and \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\). If \(x\in\operatorname{bdry}C\), a nonzero supporting normal exists. More generally, if \(F\) is the minimal face of \(C\) containing \(x\), so that \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), then \[N_C(x)=\{u:F\subset\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle u,z\rangle\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal cone is empty outside the set. At a relative-interior point it contains exactly the vectors orthogonal to the affine hull; for a full-dimensional interior point this reduces to zero. At boundary points it contains supporting directions. On the relative interior of a face, the normal cone consists of directions whose supporting face contains that entire minimal face.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x\in C\), \[u\in N_C(x)\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle u,z\rangle.\]
The tangent and normal cones are polar: \[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ.\]
special_cases_latex: For an affine subspace \(x_0+V\), the normal cone is \(V^\perp\) at every feasible point.
For the Euclidean unit ball, \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\) when \(\|x\|<1\), and \(N_C(x)=\mathbb{R}_+x\) when \(\|x\|=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Lower-dimensional feasible sets have nonzero normal directions even at relative-interior points.
Normal cones are constant on the relative interior of each face whenever the displayed minimal-face characterization applies.
boundary_notes: Boundary means relative to the ambient space; lower-dimensional sets have empty ordinary interior.
The stated supporting-normal existence uses finite dimensionality and closed convexity.

notation.meaning: linear subspace parallel to the affine hull of the set

children.top_down_role: Support functions as indicator conjugates and subdifferential values as maximizing faces.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Functions, Indicator Conjugacy, and Maximizing Faces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support geometry; the exposed face may be empty for an unbounded set when the finite supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support function is \[\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle.\] It is the conjugate of the indicator, \(\sigma_C=\iota_C^*\), and its subdifferential is the maximizing face \[\partial\sigma_C(u)=F_C(u):=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}.\] Equivalently, \[x\in\partial\sigma_C(u)\iff u\in\partial\iota_C(x)=N_C(x).\] Thus the subdifferential value of the support function is exactly the set of contact points between \(C\) and the supporting hyperplane with normal \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function records the largest pairing with a direction. Because it is the conjugate of the indicator, its subdifferential consists of all points that attain that largest pairing. These points form the exposed face selected by the direction. The relation is symmetric: a point lies in the support face for \(u\) exactly when \(u\) is normal to the set there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial\sigma_C(u)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle=F_C(u),\qquad x\in F_C(u)\iff u\in N_C(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in F_C(u)\iff \sigma_C(u)+\iota_C(x)=\langle u,x\rangle.\]
If \(F_C(u)\neq\varnothing\), then \[F_C(u)=C\cap\{x:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(u=0\), \(F_C(0)=C\) and \(\partial\sigma_C(0)=C\).
If \(C\) is compact, \(F_C(u)\) is nonempty for every \(u\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The support function is differentiable at an interior point of its domain exactly when the corresponding maximizing face is a singleton.
Flat supported portions of \(C\) appear as multivalued subdifferentials of \(\sigma_C\).
boundary_notes: If \(\sigma_C(u)=+\infty\), there is no finite supporting hyperplane in direction \(u\).
A finite support value need not be attained for every closed unbounded convex set.

notation.meaning: exposed face selected by the supporting direction

children.title: Support-Face Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Face geometry selected by supporting directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed Faces Selected by Supporting Directions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric exposed-face definition and its normal-cone incidence relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support face of \(C\) exposed by \(u\) is \[F_C(u)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle=C\cap H_C(u),\] where \[H_C(u)=\{x:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\] is the supporting hyperplane when the maximum is attained. The set \(F_C(u)\) is a face: if \((1-t)x_0+tx_1\in F_C(u)\) for \(x_0,x_1\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), then \(x_0,x_1\in F_C(u)\). Its incidence with normal geometry is \[x\in F_C(u)\iff u\in N_C(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting direction \(u\) selects all points of \(C\) at which the linear functional \(\langle u,\cdot\rangle\) is largest. Their intersection with the supporting hyperplane is an exposed face. Membership in this face is equivalent to \(u\) being a normal vector at the point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[F_C(u)=\{x\in C:\sigma_C(u)=\langle u,x\rangle\}.\]
For closed convex \(C\), \[F_C(u)=\partial\sigma_C(u).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(F_C(u)=\{x\}\), then \(x\) is an exposed point of \(C\).
If \(u=0\), then every point maximizes and \(F_C(0)=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed face is a face, although not every face of a general convex set is exposed.
Positive rescaling does not change the selected face: \(F_C(\lambda u)=F_C(u)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
boundary_notes: The face is empty if the support supremum is not attained.
The zero direction exposes the whole set and does not define a proper supporting hyperplane.

notation.meaning: support face exposed by the direction

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\sigma_C(u)=\max_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\). Then
\[
\partial\sigma_C(u)=F_C(u):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle.
\]
Consequently, every selected subgradient \(x_u\in\partial\sigma_C(u)\) is a support point satisfying \(\sigma_C(u)=\langle u,x_u\rangle\). Conversely, every support maximizer is a valid subgradient of \(\sigma_C\) at \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradients of a compact convex set's support function are exactly the points maximizing the corresponding linear functional.

The set
\[
F_C(u):=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}

\[
F_C(u)=\partial\sigma_C(u)=\{x\in C:u\in N_C(x)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonunique Support Faces and Nondifferentiable Support Values
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support functions at interior domain points, where subgradients are nonempty and differentiability is characterized by singleton values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The direction \(u\) has a nonunique support face when \[F_C(u)=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\] contains at least two distinct points. Since \(F_C(u)=\partial\sigma_C(u)\), nonuniqueness is equivalent to \(\partial\sigma_C(u)\) being nonsingleton. At \(u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C)\), this is equivalent to failure of differentiability of \(\sigma_C\) at \(u\): \[|F_C(u)|>1\iff \sigma_C\text{ is not differentiable at }u.\] The directional derivative records the whole face through \[\sigma_C'(u;v)=\max_{x\in F_C(u)}\langle v,x\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support direction is nonunique when its supporting hyperplane contacts the set at more than one point. The contact set is the support function's subdifferential. At an interior point of the support function's domain, multiple contact points are exactly the obstruction to differentiability. Directional derivatives distinguish the active points by maximizing over the entire support face.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exist \(x_1\neq x_2\) in \(C\) with \(\langle u,x_1\rangle=\langle u,x_2\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\).
The supporting hyperplane \(\{x:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\) meets \(C\) in a nontrivial convex set.
special_cases_latex: For a polytope, a direction normal to an edge or higher-dimensional facet produces a nonunique support face.
For a strictly convex compact set, every nonzero support direction has a singleton support face.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonunique support face yields multiple normal-contact points sharing the same normal direction.
Piecewise-linear support functions are nondifferentiable where their active maximizing vertices are not unique.
boundary_notes: At a boundary point of \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\), a singleton subdifferential need not give ordinary differentiability on an open neighborhood.
Nonattainment gives an empty face, not a nonunique face.

children.top_down_role: Reusable subgradient geometry generated by gauges, norms, dual balls, and polar sets.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge, Polar, Support, and Norm Geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polar geometry; gauges may be extended-valued unless the set is absorbing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\geq0:x\in tC\},\qquad C^\circ=\{u:\langle u,z\rangle\leq1\ \forall z\in C\}.\] The gauge–polar taxonomy is \[\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad \gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C,\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C.\] Consequently, \[\gamma_C^*=\iota_{C^\circ},\qquad \partial\gamma_C(x)=\{u\in C^\circ:\langle u,x\rangle=\gamma_C(x)\}\] whenever \(\gamma_C(x)\) is finite. If \(C\) is additionally absorbing, bounded, and centrally symmetric, \(\gamma_C\) is a norm, and \(C^\circ\) is the closed unit ball of its dual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge measures the smallest dilation of \(C\) containing a point. The polar collects all linear functionals bounded by one on \(C\). For a closed convex set containing zero, the gauge is the support function of the polar, and polarity is involutive. Symmetric bounded absorbing sets produce norms, with the polar serving as the dual unit ball.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\},\qquad C^\circ=\{u:\sigma_C(u)\leq1\}.\]
\[u\in\partial\gamma_C(x)\iff u\in C^\circ\text{ and }x\in N_{C^\circ}(u)\text{ in the corresponding support relation}.\]
special_cases_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\), set polarity reduces to cone polarity after accounting for homogeneity.
For a norm unit ball \(B\), \(\gamma_B=\|\cdot\|\) and \(\sigma_B=\|\cdot\|_*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Gauge subgradients are polar vectors saturating the polar inequality.
Smoothness or flatness of a gauge is controlled by exposed faces of the polar set.
boundary_notes: Without central symmetry, a finite gauge need not satisfy \(\gamma_C(x)=\gamma_C(-x)\) and is not a norm.
Without absorption, \(\gamma_C\) can equal \(+\infty\); without boundedness, it may vanish in nonzero recession directions.

children.title: Norm Dual-Ball Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Norming-functional and dual-ball organization of norm subdifferentials.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Norm Subgradients as Norming Functionals in the Dual Ball
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) carry a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), with dual norm \(\|u\|_*=\sup_{\|x\|\leq1}\langle u,x\rangle\) and dual unit ball \(B_*=\{u:\|u\|_*\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm geometry under the standard primal–dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in X\), the norm subdifferential is \[\partial\|\cdot\|(x)=\{u\in B_*:\langle u,x\rangle=\|x\|\}.\] Hence \[\partial\|\cdot\|(0)=B_*,\] while for \(x\neq0\), \[\partial\|\cdot\|(x)=\{u:\|u\|_*=1,\ \langle u,x\rangle=\|x\|\}.\] The latter elements are the norming functionals for \(x\). Equivalently, because \(\|\cdot\|=\sigma_{B_*}\), the subdifferential is the exposed face of the dual ball selected by \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradients of a norm are exactly the dual vectors of dual norm at most one that saturate the duality inequality at the given point. At zero, every dual-unit vector is a subgradient. At a nonzero point, saturation forces dual norm one, so the subgradients are precisely the norming functionals and form an exposed face of the dual ball.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x\neq0\), \[u\in\partial\|\cdot\|(x)\iff \|u\|_*=1\text{ and }\langle u,x\rangle=\|x\|.\]
\[\partial\|\cdot\|(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in B_*}\langle u,x\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: For the Euclidean norm and \(x\neq0\), \(\partial\|\cdot\|_2(x)=\{x/\|x\|_2\}\).
For \(\|x\|_1\), coordinates of a subgradient equal \(\operatorname{sign}(x_i)\) when \(x_i\neq0\) and lie in \([-1,1]\) when \(x_i=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The norm is differentiable at \(x\neq0\) exactly when \(x\) exposes a singleton face of \(B_*\).
Strict convexity of the dual ball implies uniqueness of the norming functional for each nonzero primal point.
boundary_notes: The subdifferential at zero is never a singleton in a nonzero-dimensional space.
In a general Banach space the same formula uses the continuous dual, but norm-attaining functionals and differentiability require the appropriate infinite-dimensional distinctions.

children.title: Gauge-Polar Duality
children.top_down_role: Gauge subgradients organized through polar and supporting-set representations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge, Polar Set, and Supporting Polar Face
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex with \(0\in C\). The Euclidean pairing is \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and extended-real values are permitted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex gauge geometry; the gauge may be extended-valued when \(0\notin\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gauge and polar of \(C\) are
\[\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\lambda>0:x\in\lambda C\},\qquad C^\circ:=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle s,c\rangle\leq1\ \forall c\in C\},\]
with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Gauge-polar duality is
\[\gamma_C(x)=\sigma_{C^\circ}(x):=\sup_{s\in C^\circ}\langle s,x\rangle.\]
Consequently, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C\),
\[\partial\gamma_C(x)=\{s\in C^\circ:\langle s,x\rangle=\gamma_C(x)\}.\]
Thus a gauge subgradient is exactly a polar-feasible vector whose defining polar inequality supports the gauge at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set \(C\) containing the origin, its gauge is the least nonnegative dilation needed to contain a point, while its polar consists of vectors whose pairing with every point of \(C\) is at most one. The gauge equals the support function of the polar. At any point where the gauge is finite, its subdifferential is the exposed supporting face of the polar selected by that point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[s\in\partial\gamma_C(x)\iff \langle s,c\rangle\leq1\ \forall c\in C\quad\text{and}\quad\langle s,x\rangle=\gamma_C(x).\]
\[\gamma_C(x)=\max_{s\in C^\circ}\langle s,x\rangle\quad\text{whenever the displayed maximum is attained.}\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is the unit ball of a norm, then \(C^\circ\) is the dual unit ball and \(\gamma_C\) is that norm.
At \(x=0\), \(\partial\gamma_C(0)=C^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(s\in\partial\gamma_C(x)\) supplies the global inequality \(\gamma_C(y)\geq\gamma_C(x)+\langle s,y-x\rangle\).
If \(\gamma_C(x)>0\), the normalized point \(x/\gamma_C(x)\) lies on a supporting hyperplane of \(C\) with normal \(s\).
boundary_notes: If \(0\notin\operatorname{int}C\), the gauge need not be finite everywhere.
This polar-set convention uses the level-one inequality and differs from negative polar-cone notation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential Representation of a Minkowski Gauge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact gauge-subgradient representation at the origin and at every point where the gauge is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty, closed, and convex with 0\in Q. Define \psi_Q(x):=\inf\{t>0:x\in tQ\}, with \inf\varnothing:=+\infty, and \mathcal{P}_Q:=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle g,z\rangle\le 1\ \forall z\in Q\}. Then \partial\psi_Q(0)=\mathcal{P}_Q. Moreover, for every x\in\mathbb{R}^n such that \psi_Q(x)<+\infty, \partial\psi_Q(x)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{g\in\mathcal{P}_Q}\langle g,x\rangle=\{g\in\mathcal{P}_Q:\langle g,x\rangle=\psi_Q(x)\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set containing the origin, the subdifferential of its Minkowski gauge at zero is its polar. At every point where the gauge is finite, the subgradients are exactly the polar vectors whose inner product with the point equals the gauge value.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\). For \(\varepsilon\geq0\), \(\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\) denotes the convex \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global convex minimization in finite dimensions, including extended-valued formulations of constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An exact subgradient optimality certificate at \(x\) is the membership
\[0\in\partial F(x).\]
An \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate is
\[0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x),\qquad \partial_\varepsilon F(x):=\{g:F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.\]
These certificates have the value interpretations
\[0\in\partial F(x)\iff F(x)=\inf_yF(y),\]
\[0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\iff F(x)\leq\inf_yF(y)+\varepsilon.\]
The exact certificate is therefore necessary and sufficient for global optimality, while the approximate certificate is necessary and sufficient for an objective-value error at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex objective, exact subgradient stationarity means that zero belongs to the ordinary subdifferential. Approximate stationarity in the value-certificate sense means that zero belongs to the epsilon-subdifferential. The first condition is equivalent to global minimality, and the second is equivalent to the point's objective value being within epsilon of the global infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\iff F(x)-\inf F\leq\varepsilon,\quad\text{with the exact case obtained at }\varepsilon=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\iff F(y)\geq F(x)-\varepsilon\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
\[x\in\operatorname*{argmin}F\iff0\in\partial F(x).\]
special_cases_latex: For differentiable convex \(F\), the exact certificate reduces to \(\nabla F(x)=0\).
For \(F=f+\delta_C\), the same definitions encode constrained minimization over \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact stationarity has no distinction between local and global optimality in this convex setting.
The approximate certificate directly controls objective error without requiring a norm on subgradients.
boundary_notes: A small-norm element of \(\partial F(x)\) is a different approximate-stationarity notion and does not by itself imply the same value bound without additional geometry.
For nonconvex objectives, zero-subgradient conditions generally cease to be sufficient for global optimality.

children.title: Convex Fermat Optimality Principle
children.top_down_role: The foundational subdifferential characterization of convex minimizers and its principal formulations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Fermat Stationarity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, and let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained global minimization of a proper convex function; no differentiability is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex Fermat optimality principle is the equivalence
\[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\iff0\in\partial f(\bar x),\]
where
\[\partial f(\bar x):=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(y)\geq f(\bar x)+\langle g,y-\bar x\rangle\ \forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.\]
Whenever the directional derivative \(f'(\bar x;d)\) is defined in the standard convex sense, the same condition is equivalently
\[f'(\bar x;d)\geq0\qquad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
Thus the Fermat condition is both necessary and sufficient, and it characterizes a global minimizer rather than merely a local stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point minimizes a proper convex function globally exactly when zero is one of its subgradients there. Equivalently, every directional derivative at the point is nonnegative. This is the nonsmooth convex form of the classical Fermat condition.
assumptions_latex: For the directional formulation, \(f'(\bar x;d)\) is the one-sided convex directional derivative.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[0\in\partial f(\bar x)\iff f(y)\geq f(\bar x)\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
\[f'(\bar x;\cdot)=\sigma_{\partial f(\bar x)}(\cdot)\quad\text{and}\quad \sigma_{\partial f(\bar x)}\geq0.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), then \(\partial f(\bar x)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)\}\), so the condition is \(\nabla f(\bar x)=0\).
Every local minimizer of a convex function is global.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(0\notin\partial f(\bar x)\) and the subdifferential can be strictly separated from zero, a direction \(d\) exists with \(f'(\bar x;d)<0\).
The minimizer set is convex whenever it is nonempty.
boundary_notes: The equivalence is a convex result; for a general nonconvex function, stationarity is not sufficient for global minimality.
At points outside \(\operatorname{dom}f\), the displayed subdifferential is not used as an optimality certificate.

notation.meaning: One-sided convex directional derivative in direction \(d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality conditions for the weighted Fermat-Weber problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes optimality separately away from the site set and at an individual site; the data assumptions remain those of the previously defined problem (FW), which are not reproduced in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the data $(a_i,\omega_i)_{i=1}^m$ and site set $\mathcal A$ of problem $\mathrm{(FW)}$, under the standing assumptions of that problem, a point $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbb R^d$ is optimal if and only if either
\[
\mathbf{x}^*\notin\mathcal A
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i\frac{\mathbf{x}^*-a_i}{\|\mathbf{x}^*-a_i\|_2}=0,
\]
or there exists $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ such that
\[
\mathbf{x}^*=a_j
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left\|\sum_{\substack{i=1\\i\ne j}}^m\omega_i\frac{\mathbf{x}^*-a_i}{\|\mathbf{x}^*-a_i\|_2}\right\|_2\leq\omega_j.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate solves the weighted Fermat-Weber problem exactly when the weighted unit directions balance to zero away from the sites, or, at a site, the norm of the contribution from all other sites does not exceed that site's weight.
assumptions_latex: (a_i,\omega_i)_{i=1}^m\text{ and }\mathcal A\text{ satisfy the standing assumptions of }\mathrm{(FW)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-Piece Certificate for Minimizing a Finite Maximum of Affine Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferential representation and necessary-and-sufficient global-optimality certificate for an unconstrained finite max-affine objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), define \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{a_i^Tx+b_i\}\), and set \(I(x)=\{i:f(x)=a_i^Tx+b_i\}\). Then \[\partial f(x)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i:\lambda_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\right\}=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}.\] Moreover, \(x^*\) minimizes \(f\) if and only if there exists \(\lambda\in\Delta_m\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i=0,\qquad \lambda_j=0\quad(j\notin I(x^*)).\] Equivalently, if the rows of \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) are \(a_i^T\), then \[A^T\lambda=0,\qquad \lambda_j\bigl(a_j^Tx^*+b_j-f(x^*)\bigr)=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,m).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite maximum of affine functions is the convex hull of the active slopes. A point is globally optimal exactly when a convex combination of its active slopes is zero, equivalently when simplex multipliers satisfy the stated zero-gradient and complementarity system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unconstrained Convex Minimizer and Stationarity Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite and convex. Define the optimal value \(f_\star:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued unconstrained convex optimization in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unconstrained convex minimization problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x).\]
Its solution set is
\[X_\star:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)=f_\star\}.\]
Convex subgradient stationarity identifies this set exactly:
\[X_\star=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:0\in\partial f(x)\}.\]
Equivalently, \(x\in X_\star\) precisely when the affine function of slope zero supports \(f\) at \(x\), namely \(f(y)\geq f(x)\) for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unconstrained convex minimization seeks the smallest value of a finite convex function over the whole Euclidean space. Its solution set consists exactly of the points whose subdifferential contains zero. At such a point, the constant affine function through the objective value is a global supporting minorant.
assumptions_latex: The solution-set identity remains meaningful when \(X_\star\) is empty.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in X_\star\iff f(y)\geq f(x)\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
\[x\in X_\star\iff f'(x;d)\geq0\quad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
special_cases_latex: For smooth convex \(f\), \(X_\star=\{x:\nabla f(x)=0\}\).
For strictly convex \(f\), \(X_\star\) contains at most one point.
immediate_consequences_latex: If nonempty, \(X_\star\) is convex.
Any local minimizer belongs to \(X_\star\).
boundary_notes: Finiteness does not ensure existence of a minimizer; coercivity or compactness-type assumptions are separate existence conditions.
Stationarity identifies minimizers but does not assert uniqueness without stronger convexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-to-Global Optimality and Uniqueness for Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict convexity gives uniqueness only conditionally on existence. The gradient characterization applies on an open convex domain where the gradient at the candidate is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be convex and let f:X\to\mathbb{R} be convex. Every local minimum of f over X is a global minimum over X. If f is strictly convex, then |\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)|\le 1. If X is open and \nabla f(x^*) exists for x^*\in X, then x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x) if and only if \nabla f(x^*)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator Reformulation of a Convex Constraint
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real reformulation of constrained convex minimization; closedness of \(C\) is added when normal-cone identities are invoked.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex indicator of \(C\) is
\[\delta_C(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\]
The constrained problem and its indicator form are identical:
\[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(f(x)+\delta_C(x)\bigr),\]
with the same minimizers. Hence \(\bar x\) solves the constrained problem exactly when
\[0\in\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x).\]
If an exact sum rule is valid at \(\bar x\), then \(\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\), yielding the decomposed certificate \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex constraint is encoded by adding its extended-real indicator to the objective. The resulting unconstrained extended-real problem has exactly the same values and minimizers as the original constrained problem. Fermat stationarity applies to the summed objective. When the appropriate subdifferential sum rule is exact, this stationarity condition decomposes into an objective subgradient plus a feasible-set normal.
assumptions_latex: For the normal-cone decomposition, \(C\) is closed and an exact sum-rule qualification holds.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f(x)+\delta_C(x)=f(x)\ \text{on }C,\qquad f(x)+\delta_C(x)=+\infty\ \text{off }C.\]
Under exact calculus, \[0\in\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\iff\exists g\in\partial f(\bar x): -g\in N_C(\bar x).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(\delta_C\equiv0\) and the form reduces to unconstrained minimization.
If \(f\equiv0\), every feasible point minimizes \(f+\delta_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Constraints and objectives can be handled by a single extended-real convex function.
The identity \(\partial\delta_C(x)=N_C(x)\) connects indicator calculus to normal geometry.
boundary_notes: The equality \(\partial(f+\delta_C)=\partial f+N_C\) must not be asserted without an applicable exactness condition in general extended-valued settings.
An empty feasible intersection makes the summed function improper.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composite Convex Optimality Inclusion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable, and let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex composite minimization with a smooth finite component and a possibly nonsmooth extended-valued component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the composite objective
\[F(x):=g(x)+h(x),\]
the composite optimality inclusion at \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}h\) is
\[0\in\nabla g(\bar x)+\partial h(\bar x).\]
Equivalently, there exists \(v\in\partial h(\bar x)\) satisfying
\[\nabla g(\bar x)+v=0.\]
Because the finite differentiable convex term has \(\partial g(\bar x)=\{\nabla g(\bar x)\}\) and the exact sum rule applies, this inclusion is equivalent to \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\), and hence to \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex objective formed by adding a differentiable finite convex function and a proper closed convex function, optimality is expressed by the inclusion of zero in the gradient of the smooth term plus the subdifferential of the nonsmooth term. Equivalently, a subgradient of the nonsmooth term cancels the smooth gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is finite, convex, and differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[-\nabla g(\bar x)\in\partial h(\bar x).\]
\[h(y)\geq h(\bar x)-\langle\nabla g(\bar x),y-\bar x\rangle\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(h=\delta_C\), the inclusion becomes \(-\nabla g(\bar x)\in N_C(\bar x)\).
If \(h\equiv0\), it becomes \(\nabla g(\bar x)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The inclusion separates the certificate into a smooth gradient and a nonsmooth subgradient.
Any solution of the inclusion is a global minimizer under the stated convex assumptions.
boundary_notes: For a nonconvex smooth term, the same inclusion is generally only a stationarity condition.
If neither summand is finite or continuous at an appropriate point, an exact sum formula may require qualification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent, Normal, and Directional Forms of Convex Optimality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex; let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite and convex; and let \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional constrained convex minimization with a finite-valued convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The first-order geometry at \(\bar x\) is described by
\[T_C(\bar x):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-\bar x),\qquad N_C(\bar x):=\{s:\langle s,y-\bar x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C\}.\]
The constrained convex optimality condition admits the equivalent organizations
\[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x),\]
\[f'(\bar x;y-\bar x)\geq0\quad\forall y\in C,\]
\[f'(\bar x;d)\geq0\quad\forall d\in T_C(\bar x),\]
\[0\in\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x).\]
These are respectively the primal, feasible-displacement, tangent-direction, and dual normal-cone forms of the same first-order certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite convex objective minimized over a closed convex set, optimality can be organized in four equivalent ways: global minimality, nonnegative directional change along every feasible displacement, nonnegative directional change on the tangent cone, or cancellation of an objective subgradient by a feasible-set normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C}f\iff f'(\bar x;d)\geq0\ \forall d\in T_C(\bar x)\iff0\in\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[0\in\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\iff-\partial f(\bar x)\cap N_C(\bar x)\neq\varnothing.\]
\[f'(\bar x;y-\bar x)\geq0\quad\forall y\in C.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(T_C(\bar x)=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(N_C(\bar x)=\{0\}\).
If \(f\) is differentiable, the dual form is \(-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C(\bar x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A vector \(d\in T_C(\bar x)\) with \(f'(\bar x;d)<0\) certifies failure of optimality.
The normal and tangent descriptions are polar duals.
boundary_notes: The exact dual equivalence is stated here for a finite-valued objective, matching the cited result.
For general extended-valued objectives, relative-interior or continuity qualifications may be required when decomposing an indicator-form subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Necessary and sufficient subgradient optimality conditions on the simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the qualified convex optimality rule with the support-coordinate geometry of the unit simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]$ be proper and convex, and suppose
\[
\operatorname{ri}(\Delta_n)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\ne\varnothing.
\]
Then, for every $\mathbf{x}^*\in\Delta_n$,
\[
\mathbf{x}^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf{x}\in\Delta_n}f(\mathbf{x})
\]
if and only if there exist $\mathbf g\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}^*)$ and $\mu\in\mathbb R$ such that, for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$,
\[
g_i=\mu\quad\text{if }x_i^*>0,
\qquad
g_i\geq\mu\quad\text{if }x_i^*=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the relative-interior qualification, a simplex point minimizes a proper convex function exactly when it has a subgradient that is constant on its positive support and no smaller outside that support.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf{x}^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf{x}\in\Delta_n}f(\mathbf{x})\iff\exists\mathbf g\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}^*),\exists\mu\in\mathbb R:\forall i,\ x_i^*>0\Rightarrow g_i=\mu,\ x_i^*=0\Rightarrow g_i\geq\mu

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational-inequality form of constrained convex optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses qualified constrained convex optimality through a supporting subgradient inequality over every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]$ be proper and convex, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb E$ be convex with
\[
\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(C)\ne\varnothing.
\]
Then, for every $\mathbf{x}^*\in C$,
\[
\mathbf{x}^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf{x}\in C}f(\mathbf{x})
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\,\mathbf g\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}^*)\text{ such that }
\langle\mathbf g,\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^*\rangle\geq0
\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in C.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the relative-interior qualification, a feasible point is optimal exactly when it has a subgradient whose inner product with every feasible displacement is nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate characterization of a simplex variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts the variational inequality over the unit simplex into equality on the support and inequality off the support. The extract leaves the ambient quantification of $\mathbf g$ implicit; the natural quantification $\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^n$ is made explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the setting $C=\Delta_n\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, for every $\mathbf{x}^*\in\Delta_n$ and $\mathbf g\in\mathbb R^n$,
\[
\mathbf g^T(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^*)\geq0\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\Delta_n
\]
holds if and only if there exists $\mu\in\mathbb R$ such that, for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$,
\[
g_i=\mu\quad\text{if }x_i^*>0,
\qquad
g_i\geq\mu\quad\text{if }x_i^*=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector satisfies the variational inequality at a simplex point exactly when all coordinates on the point's support equal a common value and every coordinate outside the support is at least that value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall\mathbf{x}\in\Delta_n,\ \mathbf g^T(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^*)\geq0\right]\iff\left[\exists\mu\in\mathbb R:\forall i,\ x_i^*>0\Rightarrow g_i=\mu,\ x_i^*=0\Rightarrow g_i\geq\mu\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a convex function $f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]$ and a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb E$, the associated constrained convex optimization problem is
\[
\min\{f(\mathbf{x}):\mathbf{x}\in C\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained convex optimization problem minimizes an extended-valued convex function over a convex feasible set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Cone Stationarity Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite and convex, and fix \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact constrained convex stationarity expressed in dual normal geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The normal cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[N_C(\bar x):=\{n\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle n,y-\bar x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C\}.\]
A normal-cone optimality certificate is a pair \((g,n)\) satisfying
\[g\in\partial f(\bar x),\qquad n\in N_C(\bar x),\qquad g+n=0.\]
Equivalently,
\[0\in\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\quad\text{or}\quad -g\in N_C(\bar x)\text{ for some }g\in\partial f(\bar x).\]
Under the stated convex assumptions, such a certificate exists exactly when \(\bar x\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal-cone certificate consists of an objective subgradient and a feasible-set normal that cancel each other. The normal inequality means the negative subgradient points outward from every feasible displacement. For a finite convex objective on a closed convex feasible set, existence of this pair is equivalent to global constrained optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\iff\exists g\in\partial f(\bar x)\text{ with }-g\in N_C(\bar x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\exists g\in\partial f(\bar x):\langle g,y-\bar x\rangle\geq0\quad\forall y\in C.\]
\[-\partial f(\bar x)\cap N_C(\bar x)\neq\varnothing.\]
special_cases_latex: For differentiable \(f\), the condition is \(-\nabla f(\bar x)\in N_C(\bar x)\).
If \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(N_C(\bar x)=\{0\}\), so the condition reduces to \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The certificate rules out a feasible descent direction.
The normal component records the geometric reaction of the constraint set.
boundary_notes: At \(x\notin C\), the normal cone is conventionally empty and cannot certify feasibility.
For nonconvex feasible sets, other normal cones lead to different and generally only necessary stationarity notions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent stationarity conditions for a convex-set constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes composite stationarity to a convex constraint represented by an indicator function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{E}\) be nonempty and convex, set \(g=\delta_C\), and consider \(\min\{f(x):x\in C\}\). If \(x^*\in C\) and \(f\) is differentiable at \(x^*\), then \(x^*\) is stationary if and only if \(-\nabla f(x^*)\in\partial\delta_C(x^*)=N_C(x^*)\), equivalently if and only if \(\langle\nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable objective constrained to a nonempty convex set, stationarity is equivalently a normal-cone inclusion or a variational inequality against every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ stationary}\Longleftrightarrow-\nabla f(x^*)\in N_C(x^*)\Longleftrightarrow\langle\nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\ge0\quad\forall x\in C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Softmax solution of entropy-linear simplex minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An explicit optimizer formula under the stated interior-attainment assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1\}\). Consider \(\min_{x\in\Delta_n}\bigl\{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i-\sum_{i=1}^n y_i x_i\bigr\}\). If an optimal solution \(x^*\) exists and satisfies \(x_i^*>0\) for every \(i\), then \(x_i^*=\frac{e^{y_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^n e^{y_j}}\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an entropy-minus-linear objective on the probability simplex, any strictly positive optimal solution is the softmax of the given vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]$ be proper and convex, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb E$ be convex with
\[
\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(C)\ne\varnothing.

\[
\mathbf{x}^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf{x}\in C}f(\mathbf{x})

\exists\,\mathbf g\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}^*)\text{ such that }-\mathbf g\in N_C(\mathbf{x}^*).
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polarity of Feasible, Tangent, and Normal Directions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex and let \(x\in C\). For a cone \(K\), use the negative polar \(K^\circ:=\{s:\langle s,d\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-set geometry using the negative polar-cone convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone of feasible directions and tangent cone at \(x\) are
\[D_C(x):=\{d:\exists\delta>0\ \text{such that }x+td\in C\ \forall t\in[0,\delta]\},\]
\[T_C(x):=\operatorname{cl}D_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-x).\]
The normal cone is the polar of the tangent cone:
\[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ=\{s:\langle s,d\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in T_C(x)\}.\]
Since \(T_C(x)\) is closed and convex, bipolarity also gives
\[T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.\]
Thus nonnegative first-order change on feasible directions and a cancelling normal vector are polar forms of constrained optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set, feasible directions are those that remain feasible for a short positive step, and their closure is the tangent cone. The normal cone is exactly the negative polar of the tangent cone, while the tangent cone is the negative polar of the normal cone. This polarity converts directional inequalities into normal-vector certificates.
assumptions_latex: Polar cones use the inequality \(\langle s,d\rangle\leq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[s\in N_C(x)\iff\langle s,y-x\rangle\leq0\quad\forall y\in C.\]
\[d\in T_C(x)\iff\langle s,d\rangle\leq0\quad\forall s\in N_C(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(T_C(x)=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\).
If \(C=K\) is a closed convex cone and \(x=0\), then \(T_K(0)=K\) and \(N_K(0)=K^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A vector normal to \(C\) has a nonpositive pairing with every tangent direction.
Closure is essential because the raw feasible-direction cone need not be closed.
boundary_notes: For nonconvex sets, the Bouligand tangent cone need not be convex, and polar recovery from its normal cone can lose information.
The negative polar cone here is distinct from the level-one polar set used for gauges.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact, Approximate, and Separating Certificate Regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\), and let \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A taxonomy of convex first-order certificates for global optimality, near-optimality, and nonoptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Three basic certificate regimes are distinguished. An exact optimality certificate is
\[0\in\partial F(x).\]
An \(\varepsilon\)-value certificate is
\[0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x),\]
which is equivalent to \(F(x)\leq\inf F+\varepsilon\). A separation certificate of nonoptimality is a direction \(d\) such that
\[\sigma_{\partial F(x)}(d)=F'(x;d)<0.\]
When \(F=f+\delta_C\), exact certificates may be represented by a primal-dual pair \((g,n)\) with \(g\in\partial f(x)\), \(n\in N_C(x)\), and \(g+n=0\), provided the exact decomposition is valid. The regimes respectively certify optimality, bounded value error, or a first-order descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex first-order certificates fall into three principal regimes. Exact stationarity certifies global optimality. Epsilon-subgradient stationarity certifies a global objective-value error no larger than epsilon. Strict separation of the subdifferential from zero produces a direction with negative directional derivative and therefore certifies nonoptimality. In constrained problems, an exact certificate can often be decomposed into primal subgradient and dual normal components.
assumptions_latex: A decomposed constrained certificate additionally requires a valid exact sum rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\in\partial F(x)\Rightarrow x\text{ is optimal},\quad0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\iff F(x)-\inf F\leq\varepsilon,\quad F'(x;d)<0\Rightarrow x\text{ is not optimal}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Exact: \[F(y)\geq F(x)\quad\forall y.\]
Approximate: \[F(y)\geq F(x)-\varepsilon\quad\forall y.\]
Separating: \[\sup_{g\in\partial F(x)}\langle g,d\rangle<0.\]
special_cases_latex: For smooth \(F\), exact stationarity is \(\nabla F(x)=0\).
For constrained differentiable minimization, a decomposed exact certificate is \(-\nabla f(x)\in N_C(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The exact regime is the case \(\varepsilon=0\) of the value-certificate regime.
A strict separating direction is incompatible with both exact stationarity and optimality.
boundary_notes: Norm-residual certificates such as \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\leq\eta\) are another approximate regime and require separate error-bound assumptions to imply a value estimate.
The primal-dual decomposition is not automatic for arbitrary extended-valued summands.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Subgradient-Normal Stationarity Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite and convex, and let \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional constrained convex stationarity; the unconstrained case is obtained by taking \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An exact stationarity certificate for \(\min_{y\in C}f(y)\) at \(x\) is a pair \((g,n)\) satisfying
\[g\in\partial f(x),\qquad n\in N_C(x),\qquad g+n=0.\]
Equivalently, the exact stationarity residual set contains zero:
\[0\in\partial f(x)+N_C(x).\]
Under the stated convex assumptions, this condition is equivalent to
\[x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}f(y).\]
The certificate is exact because both memberships and the cancellation equality hold without tolerance or enlargement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact constrained stationarity certificate is an objective subgradient and a feasible-set normal whose sum is exactly zero. Equivalently, zero lies in the Minkowski sum of the subdifferential and normal cone. For a finite convex objective over a closed convex set, this condition is necessary and sufficient for global optimality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\exists g\in\partial f(x): -g\in N_C(x).\]
\[\exists g\in\partial f(x):\langle g,y-x\rangle\geq0\quad\forall y\in C.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), then the certificate is \(0\in\partial f(x)\).
If \(f\) is differentiable, the certificate is \(\nabla f(x)+n=0\) for some \(n\in N_C(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The exact residual \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x)+N_C(x))\) equals zero.
The certificate simultaneously establishes feasibility and first-order optimality.
boundary_notes: A zero distance to a nonclosed residual set need not imply exact membership; here the cited finite-valued convex setting yields the stated closed-sum condition.
Approximate cancellation is not an exact certificate.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the subdifferential and normal cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Subgradient Near-Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\), and let \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate global convex optimality measured by objective-value error, not merely by subgradient norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential is
\[\partial_\varepsilon F(x):=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.\]
An approximate stationarity certificate of value tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is
\[0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x).\]
It is equivalent to
\[F(y)\geq F(x)-\varepsilon\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n,\]
and hence to
\[F(x)\leq\inf_yF(y)+\varepsilon.\]
For a constrained problem, take \(F=f+\delta_C\); then the certificate includes feasibility because \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-subdifferential relaxes the global supporting-hyperplane inequality by epsilon. Approximate stationarity in the value sense means that zero belongs to this enlarged subdifferential. This happens exactly when the point's objective value is no more than epsilon above the global infimum. Constraints are included by using an indicator-augmented objective.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[F(y)\geq F(x)-\varepsilon\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
\[\varepsilon\geq F(x)-\inf F.\]
special_cases_latex: At \(\varepsilon=0\), the definition reduces to exact stationarity.
For \(F=f+\delta_C\), it is equivalent to \(x\in C\) and \(f(x)\leq\inf_{y\in C}f(y)+\varepsilon\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The sets \(\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\) increase with \(\varepsilon\).
Every exact subgradient is an \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient for every \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
boundary_notes: A certificate \(g\in\partial F(x)\) with small \(\|g\|\) is not equivalent to this value certificate without bounded-domain or growth assumptions.
The epsilon-normal set of an indicator is generally not a cone when \(\varepsilon>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential Separation and Supporting-Model Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite and convex, fix \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(S:=\partial f(x)\), a nonempty compact convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order certificates of nonoptimality and global affine lower support for finite convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A strict separation certificate for nonoptimality of \(x\) is a direction \(d\neq0\) satisfying
\[\sigma_S(d):=\sup_{g\in S}\langle g,d\rangle<0.\]
Because
\[f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d),\]
this condition is exactly \(f'(x;d)<0\), so \(d\) is a descent direction and \(x\) cannot minimize \(f\). Independently, each \(g\in\partial f(x)\) defines the global supporting model
\[m_{x,g}(y):=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\leq f(y)\quad\forall y.\]
Thus separation supplies an improvement certificate, while the supporting model supplies a globally valid affine lower-bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the compact convex subdifferential at a point can be strictly separated from the origin, the separating direction has negative pairing with every subgradient. Its directional derivative is negative, so it certifies nonoptimality. Each individual subgradient also defines an affine function supporting the objective globally from below, which can certify lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\partial f(x)\) is evaluated using the fixed Euclidean pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)<0\Rightarrow f'(x;d)<0\Rightarrow x\notin\operatorname*{argmin}f,\]
and \[m_{x,g}\leq f\quad\forall g\in\partial f(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle<0.\]
\[0\notin\partial f(x)\iff\text{there exists a strict separating direction for the compact convex set }\partial f(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable, the separation test is \(\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle<0\).
Taking \(d=-\operatorname{proj}_{S}(0)\) gives a canonical separating direction when \(0\notin S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A strict separation certificate excludes exact stationarity.
The supporting model yields \(\inf_y f(y)\geq\inf_y m_{x,g}(y)\), whenever the latter lower bound is finite over the relevant domain.
boundary_notes: A supporting model alone need not certify that its base point is optimal; zero slope is required for that conclusion in the unconstrained case.
Strict separation may fail for nonclosed or nonconvex generalized subdifferentials.

notation.meaning: Affine supporting model generated at \(x\) by \(g\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness of a Subdifferential Calculus Rule
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\) be a convex function constructed from convex data \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) by an operation for which a candidate set-valued expression \(\mathcal R(x)\) is formed from their subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of exactness for convex subdifferential rules, with finite-valued positive sums and affine precomposition as canonical instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A subdifferential calculus rule is exact at \(x\) when its constructed set equals the true subdifferential:
\[\partial f(x)=\mathcal R(x).\]
For finite convex functions \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(t_1,t_2>0\), the positive-sum rule is exact everywhere:
\[\partial(t_1f_1+t_2f_2)(x)=t_1\partial f_1(x)+t_2\partial f_2(x).\]
For an affine map \(A(x)=A_0x+b\) and finite convex \(g\), the affine-chain rule is likewise exact:
\[\partial(g\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial g(Ax).\]
Exactness means that every subgradient of the constructed function is represented by the prescribed component subgradients, not merely that the construction produces valid subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subdifferential calculus is exact at a point when the set assembled from the component subdifferentials equals the entire subdifferential of the resulting function. Positive combinations of finite convex functions and precomposition of a finite convex function by an affine map are canonical globally exact rules. Equality is stronger than a one-sided validity inclusion.
assumptions_latex: All functions in the two displayed canonical rules are finite and convex on their full Euclidean spaces.
\(A(x)=A_0x+b\) is affine and \(A_0^*\) is its adjoint.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Exactness at \(x\): \[s\in\partial f(x)\iff s\in\mathcal R(x).\]
For the sum: \[s\in\partial(t_1f_1+t_2f_2)(x)\iff s=t_1s_1+t_2s_2\text{ for some }s_i\in\partial f_i(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If one summand is differentiable, its subdifferential contribution is its gradient singleton.
If \(A\) is linear, then \(b=0\) and the same adjoint rule applies.
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact rules permit stationarity of a structured objective to be rewritten as an explicit inclusion involving component subgradients.
Repeated application yields exact formulas for finite positive sums of finite convex functions.
boundary_notes: For extended-valued functions, the same-looking equalities may require relative-interior, continuity, or other qualification conditions.
A universal inclusion is not an exact rule unless the reverse inclusion is also established.

notation.meaning: Candidate subdifferential expression assembled from component data.
Adjoint of the linear part of \(A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hierarchy of Inclusion, Qualified Equality, and Approximate Recovery
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f_1\cap\operatorname{dom}f_2\), and set \(f=f_1+f_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sum calculus used as the canonical model of qualification regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The qualification hierarchy for the sum rule consists of the following distinct levels. The universal weak relation is
\[\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x)\subseteq\partial(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
Under an exactness qualification such as
\[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_1)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2)\neq\varnothing,\]
the inclusion strengthens to equality. At positive tolerance, the approximate rule is
\[\partial_\varepsilon(f_1+f_2)(x)\supseteq\bigcup_{\substack{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\geq0\\\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2\leq\varepsilon}}\bigl(\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f_1(x)+\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f_2(x)\bigr),\]
with equality when the corresponding conjugate infimal convolution is exact, in particular under the displayed relative-interior condition. Qualification-free exact recovery can instead use closures and intersections of enlarged subdifferentials:
\[\partial(f_1+f_2)(x)=\bigcap_{0<\eta\leq\bar\eta}\operatorname{cl}\bigl(\partial_\eta f_1(x)+\partial_\eta f_2(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum-rule hierarchy separates four levels that must not be conflated: an always-valid inclusion, equality under a relative-interior or equivalent exactness qualification, an epsilon-subdifferential formula that allocates approximation error among the summands, and a qualification-free recovery formula using closures and intersections of enlarged subdifferentials.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are proper, closed, and convex.
The equality in the approximate allocation formula requires exactness of the conjugate infimal convolution; the relative-interior condition is a sufficient qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{unqualified inclusion}\ \subseteq\ \text{qualified equality},\qquad \text{and exact recovery without qualification is available through closed approximate sums.}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Qualified exactness: \[s\in\partial(f_1+f_2)(x)\iff s=s_1+s_2\text{ with }s_i\in\partial f_i(x).\]
Approximate allocation: \[s=s_1+s_2,\ s_i\in\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x),\ \varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow s\in\partial_\varepsilon(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If both functions are finite everywhere, the relative-interior condition holds automatically.
At \(\varepsilon=0\), the qualified approximate equality reduces to the exact sum rule.
immediate_consequences_latex: Failure of a qualification does not invalidate the weak inclusion.
Enlarged subdifferentials retain enough information to recover the exact sum subdifferential after closure and intersection.
boundary_notes: The relative-interior condition is sufficient, not necessary.
The closure-intersection formula is materially different from simply closing \(\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x)\).

notation.meaning: Arbitrary positive upper scale for approximate recovery.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unqualified Weak Sum Inclusion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f_1\cap\operatorname{dom}f_2\). Empty subdifferentials are allowed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification-free convex subdifferential calculus; the claim is an inclusion, not an exact formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The weak sum-calculus regime is the universally valid inclusion
\[\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x)\subseteq\partial(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
Equivalently, for every \(g_1\in\partial f_1(x)\) and \(g_2\in\partial f_2(x)\),
\[g_1+g_2\in\partial(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
Its approximate counterpart is: for \(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\geq0\),
\[\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f_1(x)+\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f_2(x)\subseteq\partial_{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
These relations require no relative-interior or continuity qualification. They assert validity of every constructed sum subgradient but do not assert that every subgradient of the sum admits such a decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without any exactness qualification, component subgradients can always be added to obtain a valid subgradient of the sum. The same is true for approximate subgradients, with their error tolerances added. This is a one-sided construction rule: the full subdifferential of the sum may contain elements that cannot be decomposed using exact component subgradients at the same point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(g_i\in\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\), then \[f_1(y)+f_2(y)\geq f_1(x)+f_2(x)+\langle g_1+g_2,y-x\rangle-(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)\quad\forall y.\]
Exact weak inclusion: \[g_i\in\partial f_i(x)\Rightarrow g_1+g_2\in\partial(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If either component subdifferential is empty, the exact left-hand side is empty and the inclusion remains valid.
When a suitable relative-interior condition holds, the exact inclusion strengthens to equality.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any computable component certificate produces a valid certificate for the summed function.
Approximation errors combine additively.
boundary_notes: The reverse inclusion can fail when domains meet without an exactness qualification.
Calling the weak inclusion an equality would lose the essential distinction encoded by this regime.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum when applied to sets of subgradients.

e\varnothing,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{cont}}(f,g):\Longleftrightarrow D_f\cap\operatorname{cont}g
e\varnothing.\]
The classical exactness qualification pair is \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{cl}}(f,g)=\{Q_{\mathrm{ri}}(f,g),Q_{\mathrm{cont}}(f,g)\}\). A pair \((f,g)\) is classically qualified when at least one member of \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{cl}}(f,g)\) holds. In that case \(f+g\) is proper and, for every \(x\in E\),
\[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper convex functions on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the classical qualification pair consists of either a common point of the relative interiors of their effective domains or a point in the domain of one function at which the other is finite and continuous. A pair is classically qualified if at least one condition holds. Under either condition, the subdifferential of the sum equals the Minkowski sum of the two subdifferentials at every point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite-dimensional \(E\), \(Q_{\mathrm{ri}}(f,g)\) is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(D_f-D_g)\).
If \(g\) is finite on all of \(E\), then \(\operatorname{cont}g=E\), so \(Q_{\mathrm{cont}}(f,g)\) holds whenever \(f\) is proper.
special_cases_latex: If both functions are finite-valued convex functions on \(E\), exactness holds everywhere without any additional domain test.

For indicator functions \(f=\iota_C\) and \(g=\iota_D\), the relative-interior condition becomes \(\operatorname{ri}C\cap\operatorname{ri}D\ne\varnothing\), and the formula becomes \(N_{C\cap D}(x)=N_C(x)+N_D(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: At every \(x\in D_f\cap D_g\), each \(u\in\partial(f+g)(x)\) admits a decomposition \(u=u_f+u_g\) with \(u_f\in\partial f(x)\) and \(u_g\in\partial g(x)\).
For positive weights \(\alpha,\beta>0\), the same qualifications yield \(\partial(\alpha f+\beta g)=\alpha\partial f+\beta\partial g\).
boundary_notes: The conditions are sufficient, not necessary; exactness may hold when both fail.
Relative interior is the finite-dimensional mechanism. Infinite-dimensional replacements such as strong relative interior belong to the generalized-interior regime.
Without qualification, only \(\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\subseteq\partial(f+g)(x)\) is automatic.

notation.meaning: Set of points at which g is finite and continuous.
Minkowski sum of subsets of the dual space.
