knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-relative-interior qualification in Hilbert space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(H)\), where \(\Gamma_0(H)\) denotes the proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions \(H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Set \(D=\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The primary generalized-interior mechanism is strong relative interior, whose definition incorporates closedness of the direction subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex set \(C\subset H\), define
\[\operatorname{core}C=\{x\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=H\},\]
\[\operatorname{sri}C=\{x\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(C-x)\},\]
\[\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=\operatorname{span}(C-x)\},\quad \operatorname{qri}C=\{x\in C:\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(C-x)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(C-x)\}.\]
The generalized-interior qualification for the pair \((f,g)\) is
\[0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g).\]
When it holds,
\[\partial(f+g)=\partial f+\partial g.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized-interior family consists of core, strong relative interior, relative interior, and quasirelative interior. For exact Hilbert-space sum calculus, the canonical qualification requires zero to belong to the strong relative interior of the difference of the effective domains. Strong relative interior means that the cone generated by the translated set equals the closed linear span of that set. Under this condition, the subdifferential of the sum is exactly the pointwise sum of the subdifferentials.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(0\in D\), the condition \(0\in\operatorname{sri}D\) means that \(\operatorname{cone}D\) is a closed linear subspace of \(H\).
In finite dimensions, \(\operatorname{sri}C=\operatorname{ri}C\), so the qualification reduces to \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{dom}g=H\), then the exact sum rule holds.
If \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\), the strong-relative-interior condition is satisfied.
For a closed linear subspace \(V\subset H\), \(\operatorname{sri}V=V\), even when \(\operatorname{int}V=\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The condition accommodates lower-dimensional closed subspace geometry that ordinary interior cannot detect.
Under the qualification, every \(u\in\partial(f+g)(x)\) splits as \(u_f+u_g\) with \(u_f\in\partial f(x)\) and \(u_g\in\partial g(x)\).
boundary_notes: Quasirelative interior is weaker than strong relative interior and does not by itself give the stated exact sum rule.
The closure in \(\overline{\operatorname{span}}(C-x)\) is essential in infinite dimensions.
The family is stated for Hilbert spaces; extensions to broader locally convex spaces require topology-specific duality hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on H.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearby-point recovery of approximate subgradients
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper closed convex. For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define \(\partial_\varepsilon f(x)=\{s:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle s,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \forall y\in\mathbb R^n\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex functions. Recovery is qualification-free but approximate: an epsilon-subgradient is represented through an exact subgradient at a nearby point with a controlled dual error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The qualification-free nearby-point recovery family is the collection of inclusions, indexed by \(\eta>0\),
\[\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\subseteq igcup_{\|y-x\|\le\eta}\left(\partial f(y)+ rac{\varepsilon}{\eta}Bight),\]
where \(B=\{u\in\mathbb R^n:\|u\|\le1\}\). Equivalently, for every \(s\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\) and every \(\eta>0\), there exist \(x_\eta\) and \(s_\eta\) such that
\[\|x_\eta-x\|\le\eta,\qquad s_\eta\in\partial f(x_\eta),\qquad\|s_\eta-s\|\le\varepsilon/\eta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient can always be recovered, without a domain qualification, from an exact subgradient evaluated at a nearby point. For every chosen radius eta, the nearby point lies within eta of the base point and the exact subgradient lies within epsilon divided by eta of the target epsilon-subgradient. The family trades primal displacement against dual error and includes the exact case when epsilon is zero.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\subseteq\bigcap_{\eta>0}\bigcup_{\|y-x\|\le\eta}\left(\partial f(y)+(\varepsilon/\eta)B\right).\]
Choosing \(\eta=\sqrt\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon>0\) gives simultaneous bounds \(\|x_\eta-x\|\le\sqrt\varepsilon\) and \(\|s_\eta-s\|\le\sqrt\varepsilon\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\varepsilon=0\), one may choose \(x_\eta=x\) and \(s_\eta=s\).
Every \(s\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\) lies in \(\overline{\partial f(\mathbb R^n)}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Approximate first-order information can be reconstructed from exact subgradients sampled away from the reference point.
The parameter \(\eta\) explicitly controls the primal-distance versus dual-error tradeoff.
boundary_notes: The recovery statement is an inclusion, not an assertion that every nearby perturbed exact subgradient is an epsilon-subgradient.
For fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), demanding a small dual error may require a large displacement.
Closedness and finite dimensionality are part of the cited formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic calculus generated by positive combinations and separable products
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex functions and let \(\alpha_i>0\). Subdifferential sums and scalar multiples are Minkowski operations on subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finite-valued convex functions. In this regime the elementary algebraic rules are exact without an additional qualification because every function is continuous everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The algebraic subdifferential calculus is the operation-preserving assignment \(f\mapsto\partial f\) specified by
\[\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_iight)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\partial f_i(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n),\]
and, for finite convex \(p:\mathbb R^r	o\mathbb R\) and \(q:\mathbb R^s	o\mathbb R\), by
\[F(x,y)=p(x)+q(y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\partial F(x,y)=\partial p(x)	imes\partial q(y).\]
Constants contribute \(\{0\}\), and multiplication by a positive scalar acts by the same scalar on the subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algebraic subdifferential calculus assigns exact set operations to positive linear combinations and separable sums. The subdifferential of a positive finite combination is the corresponding Minkowski combination of the component subdifferentials. For a function on a product space that separates as a sum of two component functions, its subdifferential is the Cartesian product of the two component subdifferentials.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A vector \(u\) belongs to \(\partial(\sum_i\alpha_i f_i)(x)\) exactly when \(u=\sum_i\alpha_i u_i\) for some \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\).
For \(F=p\oplus q\), \((u,v)\in\partial F(x,y)\) exactly when \(u\in\partial p(x)\) and \(v\in\partial q(y)\).
special_cases_latex: \(\partial(\alpha f)(x)=\alpha\partial f(x)\) for \(\alpha>0\).
\(\partial(f+c)(x)=\partial f(x)\) for every constant \(c\in\mathbb R\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If every component is differentiable at \(x\), the rule reduces to \(\nabla(\sum_i\alpha_i f_i)(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i\nabla f_i(x)\).
A separable convex minimization problem has \(0\in\partial F(x,y)\) exactly when \(0\in\partial p(x)\) and \(0\in\partial q(y)\).
boundary_notes: Negative coefficients are excluded because they need not preserve convexity and the displayed subdifferential identity can fail.
For extended-valued summands, an exact sum formula requires a qualification; only the easy inclusion is unconditional.

notation.meaning: Separable sum on the product space, (p⊕q)(x,y)=p(x)+q(y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact rules for affine value and argument perturbations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex, let \(a,b\in\mathbb R^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R\), and \(\lambda>0\). Identify linear functionals with vectors under the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional and finite-valued. These transformations inherit the subgradient structure directly and require no constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Elementary affine perturbation calculus is defined by the transformed functions
\[g(x)=\lambda f(x)+\langle a,xangle+c,\qquad h(x)=f(x+b).\]
Their subdifferentials are, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[\partial g(x)=\lambda\partial f(x)+\{a\},\qquad \partial h(x)=\partial f(x+b).\]
Combining the two operations, if \(k(x)=\lambda f(x+b)+\langle a,xangle+c\), then
\[\partial k(x)=\lambda\partial f(x+b)+\{a\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling of a convex function rescales its subdifferential, addition of an affine functional translates the subdifferential by the functional's coefficient, addition of a constant has no effect, and translation of the argument evaluates the original subdifferential at the translated point. These operations may be combined in one exact formula.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(u\in\partial k(x)\) if and only if \((u-a)/\lambda\in\partial f(x+b)\).
The graph transformation is \(\operatorname{gra}\partial k=\{(x,\lambda v+a):(x+b,v)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\}\).
special_cases_latex: With \(a=b=0\), \(\partial(\lambda f+c)=\lambda\partial f\).
With \(\lambda=1\) and \(b=0\), \(\partial(f+\langle a,\cdot\rangle+c)=\partial f+a\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(0\in\partial k(x)\) exactly when \(-a/\lambda\in\partial f(x+b)\).
If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x+b\), then \(k\) is differentiable at \(x\) with \(\nabla k(x)=\lambda\nabla f(x+b)+a\).
boundary_notes: The scalar \(\lambda\) must be positive for the stated convex subdifferential rule.
A nontrivial linear precomposition \(f(Ax+b)\) is governed by the affine chain rule, not merely by this perturbation rule.

children.title: Positive Scaling
children.top_down_role: Subgradient structure inherited under positive scalar multiplication.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex-subdifferential rule for strictly positive objective scaling.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Subdifferentials of Extended-Valued Functions p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
v\in\partial(\alpha f)(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{v}{\alpha}\in\partial f(x).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\partial(\alpha f)(x)=\alpha\,\partial f(x).
\]
Strict positivity of \(\alpha\) preserves the direction of the defining subgradient inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying a proper convex function by a strictly positive scalar multiplies every subgradient by the same scalar.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Scaling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictly Positive Convex Function on a Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the extraction's subgradient inequality exactly, including both function-value terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f be a closed convex set and let f be convex. The function f is strictly positive on Q if, for every x,y\in Q and every g\in\partial f(x), \[f(y)+f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ge 0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function is strictly positive on a closed convex set Q when, for every pair x and y in Q and every subgradient of f at x, the stated sum of two function values and the subgradient pairing is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is strictly positive on }Q\iff (\forall x,y\in Q)(\forall g\in\partial f(x))\;f(y)+f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ge 0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure of Strict Positivity under Binary Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's notion of strict positivity on a set; it is not a statement about conic strict feasibility or pointwise positive-domain metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q be a set, and let f_1,f_2:Q\to\mathbb{R} be strictly positive on Q. Then f:Q\to\mathbb{R}, defined by f(x)=\max\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\} for every x\in Q, is strictly positive on Q.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise maximum of two functions that are strictly positive on the same set is again strictly positive there.
assumptions_latex: f_1\text{ and }f_2\text{ are strictly positive on }Q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient covariance under translation of the function argument.

source_refs.locator: 1 The Elementary Mechanism p. 2
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms II: Advanced Theory and Bundle Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the translated function \(g(x)=f(x-a)\), a vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies
\[
v\in\partial g(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v\in\partial f(x-a).
\]
Hence
\[
\partial g(x)=\partial f(x-a).
\]
Translation changes the evaluation point but leaves the subgradient vectors themselves unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translating the argument shifts the point where the original subdifferential is evaluated but does not change its vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Argument Translation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
v\in\partial g(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v-a\in\partial f(x).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\partial g(x)=\partial f(x)+a.

The constant \(b\) has no effect on the subdifferential, while the linear term translates every subgradient by its slope \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding an affine functional translates the subdifferential by its slope; the constant term has no effect.

children.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exceptional behavior associated with zero or sign-changing scaling.

assumptions_latex: For zero scaling, \((0f)(x)=0\) on \(\operatorname{dom}f\) and \((0f)(x)=+\infty\) otherwise.
For the negative-scaling clause, \(\alpha<0\) and \(f\) is nonaffine and real-valued on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(\partial(0f)(x)=N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)\), which need not equal \(0\,\partial f(x)\); under the negative-scaling assumptions, \(\alpha f\) is concave and not convex, so convex subdifferential calculus does not apply to it as a convex function.

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to a convex set.
A strictly negative scaling factor in the negative-scaling clause.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the positive-scaling rule under the stated extended-real zero-scaling convention and under negative scaling of a nonaffine real-valued convex function.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Subdifferentials of Extended-Valued Functions p. 47
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms II: Advanced Theory and Bundle Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated convention, \(0f=\delta_{\operatorname{dom}f}\). Hence, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\),
\[
\partial(0f)(x)=N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x).
\]
This set need not equal \(0\,\partial f(x)\); in particular, \(0\,\partial f(x)\) is empty when \(\partial f(x)\) is empty and is \(\{0\}\) otherwise. If \(\alpha<0\) and \(f\) is nonaffine and real-valued on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(\alpha f\) is concave and not convex. Thus the positive-scaling identity has no general extension to nonpositive scalars.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated zero-scaling convention, the scaled function is the domain indicator and its subdifferential is the domain normal cone, which need not equal the zero-scaled original subdifferential. Negative scaling of a nonaffine real-valued convex function destroys convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes

children.top_down_role: Weak, exact, and closure-sensitive regimes for finite sums.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak, exact, and approximate convex sum-rule regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_i:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions with nonempty common effective domain, and set \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\). For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), use the epsilon-subdifferential \(\partial_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The family separates what holds for every proper convex sum from exact formulas requiring domain regularity and from epsilon-level decompositions requiring exact conjugate infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Moreau–Rockafellar sum-rule family consists of the following nested relations at \(x\in igcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial F(x),\]
\[\partial F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)\quad	ext{under an exactness qualification},\]
and, when the conjugate infimal convolution is exact,
\[\partial_\varepsilon F(x)= igcup_{\substack{\varepsilon_i\ge0\\sum_i\varepsilon_i\le\varepsilon}}\sum_{i=1}^m\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x).\]
In finite dimensions, \( igcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)
e\varnothing\) is a standard qualification for both exact formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau–Rockafellar family organizes sum calculus into three regimes. The sum of exact component subdifferentials is always contained in the subdifferential of the sum. Under a domain qualification this inclusion becomes equality. At the approximate level, exactness of the conjugate infimal convolution yields a union over all nonnegative allocations of the total epsilon among the summands.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sum_i\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial\!\left(\sum_i f_i\right)(x),\quad\text{with equality under qualification, and an epsilon-allocation formula under conjugate exactness}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Exactness at \(x\) means every \(u\in\partial F(x)\) can be decomposed as \(u=\sum_i u_i\) with \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\).
For two summands, conjugate exactness means \((f_1+f_2)^*(u)=\min_{u_1+u_2=u}(f_1^*(u_1)+f_2^*(u_2))\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\varepsilon=0\), the epsilon-allocation formula reduces to the exact subdifferential sum rule.
For finite-valued convex summands on \(\mathbb R^n\), exactness holds everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: Qualified first-order optimality can be written \(0\in\sum_i\partial f_i(x)\).
The epsilon formula assigns a separate error budget \(\varepsilon_i\) to each summand.
boundary_notes: The weak inclusion has the direction \(\sum_i\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial F(x)\).
The approximate equality is not qualification-free; it depends on exactness of the relevant conjugate infimal convolution.
Empty subdifferentials are permitted, so an inclusion may be strict or uninformative.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the subdifferential sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary choices \(v_i\in\partial f_i(x)\), their sum satisfies
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m v_i\in\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)
\subseteq
\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x).
\]
This inclusion requires no continuity or relative-interior qualification; only the reverse inclusion can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a common domain point, every sum of individual subgradients is a subgradient of the function sum, without any qualification condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Unqualified Sum Inclusions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualification-free exact and epsilon sum inclusions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, let \(x\in\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\), and put \(F=\sum_i f_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No relative-interior, continuity, or closed-subspace qualification is imposed. The statement records only relations valid directly from the defining subgradient inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unqualified sum inclusions are
\[\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial F(x)\]
and, for every \(\varepsilon\ge0\),
\[ igcup_{\substack{\varepsilon_i\ge0\\sum_i\varepsilon_i\le\varepsilon}}\sum_{i=1}^m\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\subseteq\partial_\varepsilon F(x).\]
Thus any selection \(u_i\in\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\) with total error at most \(\varepsilon\) produces \(\sum_i u_i\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without any qualification, component subgradients may always be added to obtain a subgradient of the sum. The same statement holds for approximate subgradients: if nonnegative component error budgets add to at most the target error, then the sum of the selected component epsilon-subgradients is a target epsilon-subgradient of the sum. No converse decomposition is asserted.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(u_i\in\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\), then \(F(y)\ge F(x)+\langle\sum_i u_i,y-x\rangle-\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) for every \(y\in E\).
The exact inclusion is the case \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_1=\cdots=\varepsilon_m=0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=2\), \(\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x)\subseteq\partial(f_1+f_2)(x)\).
If a component subdifferential is empty, the corresponding Minkowski sum is empty and the inclusion remains valid.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any computable decomposition of a dual vector into component subgradients certifies membership in the subdifferential of the total objective.
Approximate component certificates combine additively in both slope and error.
boundary_notes: The reverse inclusion can fail when the domains meet only at their boundaries.
Closure of the right-hand Minkowski sum does not automatically supply the missing converse.
This definition does not assert properness of \(F\) outside the stipulated common-domain point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the domains have a common relative-interior point, then at every \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\),
\[
\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x)
=
\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x).
\]
Thus every subgradient of the sum admits an exact decomposition \(v=\sum_{i=1}^m v_i\) with \(v_i\in\partial f_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common relative-interior domain point makes the finite convex sum rule exact, so every subgradient of the sum decomposes into individual subgradients.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact finite-sum rule under domain regularity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\Gamma_0(H)\). Set \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\) and assume the common effective domain is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex finite-sum calculus. The primary Hilbert-space condition is stated sequentially with strong relative interiors; its finite-dimensional specialization is common relative-interior intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The qualified exact finite-sum regime is defined by
\[0\in igcap_{i=2}^m\operatorname{sri}\!\left(\operatorname{dom}f_i- igcap_{j=1}^{i-1}\operatorname{dom}f_jight).\]
Under this qualification,
\[\partial F=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i.\]
In finite-dimensional \(H\), the symmetric condition
\[ igcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)
e\varnothing\]
is a standard sufficient qualification for the same identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family is in the qualified exact sum regime when each new effective domain meets the preceding common domain with strong-relative-interior regularity. Under this condition, the subdifferential of the total sum is exactly the pointwise Minkowski sum of all component subdifferentials. In finite dimensions, it is enough that all relative interiors have a common point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(m=2\), the Hilbert-space condition is \(0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2-\operatorname{dom}f_1)\).

In finite dimensions, \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2-\operatorname{dom}f_1)\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_1)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2)\ne\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: If one summand has full domain, the two-function exact rule holds.
If all summands are finite-valued on \(\mathbb R^n\), the relative-interior qualification is automatic.
For indicator functions, the rule specializes to an exact normal-cone intersection formula.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every total subgradient has a componentwise decomposition.
The optimality condition \(0\in\partial F(x)\) becomes \(0\in\sum_i\partial f_i(x)\).
boundary_notes: The displayed sequential condition depends on the ordering but is only a sufficient criterion; exactness itself is order-independent.
The rule is not valid merely from nonempty intersection of the effective domains.
In infinite dimensions, ordinary relative-interior intersection is not an adequate substitute for strong relative interior.

notation.meaning: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on H.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), where each \(f_i\) is finite convex, and let \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex and nondecreasing in each coordinate. Separately, let \(A(x)=A_0x+b\) be affine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finite-valued composition calculus. It combines affine precomposition and componentwise-monotone postcomposition, the two basic mapping transformations covered by the cited source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex composition mapping calculus assigns to \(h=g\circ F\) the exact set
\[\partial h(x)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^mho_i s_i:ho=(ho_1,\ldots,ho_m)\in\partial g(F(x)),\ s_i\in\partial f_i(x)ight\}.\]
Every \(ho\in\partial g(F(x))\) satisfies \(ho_i\ge0\). For affine precomposition of a finite convex \(q:\mathbb R^m	o\mathbb R\),
\[\partial(q\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial q(Ax).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex composition mapping calculus covers two exact transformations. For a componentwise nondecreasing convex outer function applied to a vector of finite convex inner functions, subgradients are nonnegative weighted sums of inner subgradients, with weights taken from the outer subdifferential. For a finite convex function precomposed with an affine map, the outer subdifferential is pulled back by the adjoint of the linear part.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The first formula is the union of Minkowski sums \(\sum_i\rho_i\partial f_i(x)\) over \(\rho\in\partial g(F(x))\).
When every function is differentiable, it becomes \(\nabla(g\circ F)(x)=\sum_i(\partial_i g)(F(x))\nabla f_i(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=1\), the first formula gives monotone scalar composition.
For \(g(y)=\max_i y_i\), it gives the active-index finite-maximum rule.
For linear \(A\), the affine formula has \(b=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Coordinatewise monotonicity forces the outer subgradient weights to be nonnegative, preserving convex combinations of inner subgradient inequalities.
Affine and monotone postcomposition rules can be nested when their respective hypotheses hold.
boundary_notes: If the outer function is not monotone on the relevant range, convexity of \(g\circ F\) and the displayed rule can fail.
Extended-valued outer functions require domain qualifications absent from this finite-valued formulation.
A general cone order requires a cone-dual formulation beyond the componentwise specialization stated here.

Vector mapping with convex scalar components.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine pullback chain-rule family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex, let \(A_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and define \(A(x)=A_0x+b\) and \(f=h\circ A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-valued convex outer functions. The family distinguishes the unconditional pullback inclusion from exactness under range-domain regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine chain-rule family is
\[A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\subseteq\partial(h\circ A)(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n),\]
with exactness whenever
\[(b+\operatorname{ran}A_0)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h)
e\varnothing.\]
Under this qualification,
\[\partial(h\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an affine precomposition, pulling an outer subgradient back through the adjoint always produces a subgradient of the composite. The reverse representation is guaranteed when the affine range meets the relative interior of the outer effective domain. The exact chain rule then identifies every composite subgradient with the adjoint image of an outer subgradient.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The qualification is \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h-b-\operatorname{ran}A_0)\).
Exactness means \(u\in\partial(h\circ A)(x)\) if and only if there exists \(v\in\partial h(Ax)\) with \(u=A_0^*v\).
special_cases_latex: If \(h\) is finite-valued on \(\mathbb R^m\), exactness is automatic.
If \(A_0\) is surjective, its affine range is \(\mathbb R^m\), so exactness holds whenever \(h\) is proper.
If \(h\) is polyhedral, meeting \(\operatorname{dom}h\) is sufficient in the cited finite-dimensional rule.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(h\) is differentiable at \(Ax\), then \(h\circ A\) is differentiable at \(x\) with gradient \(A_0^*\nabla h(Ax)\).
The kernel of \(A_0\) is automatically annihilated by every subgradient represented through the exact chain rule.
boundary_notes: Injectivity of \(A_0\) alone does not ensure that its range meets the relative interior of \(\operatorname{dom}h\).
If \(Ax\notin\operatorname{dom}h\), both sides are interpreted at a point where the composite is infinite and its subdifferential is empty.
Outside the qualification, the displayed inclusion can be strict.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(f:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(T(x)=Ax+b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(A\) is surjective, then \(\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial f(Tx)\); if \(A\) is injective, then \(\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial_S(f|_S)(Tx)\), where \(S=b+\operatorname{ran}A\).

notation.meaning: Affine mapping from X to Y.
Adjoint of the linear part A.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct finite-dimensional formulas for surjective maps and injective parametrizations of affine subspaces.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Pre-Composition with an Affine Mapping p. 56

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(A:X\to Y\) is surjective, then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}(f\circ T)\),
\[
\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial f(Ax+b).
\]
If \(A\) is injective, set \(S=b+\operatorname{ran}A\) and regard \(f|_S\) as a convex function on \(S\). Since \(T:X\to S\) is an affine bijection,
\[
\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial_S(f|_S)(Ax+b).
\]
For bijective \(A\), both formulas coincide with the ordinary ambient-space chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Surjective affine maps give the usual adjoint chain rule. Injective maps give the same rule after restricting the outer function to the mapped affine subspace.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directly exact affine-mapping regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A(x)=A_0x+b\) map \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R^m\), and let \(h:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine precomposition. The definition collects elementary structural cases in which the exact adjoint chain rule is immediate from full domain, surjectivity, or polyhedral feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The elementary exact affine-mapping regimes are the following alternatives:
\[(\mathrm F)\quad\operatorname{dom}h=\mathbb R^m;\qquad (\mathrm S)\quad\operatorname{ran}A_0=\mathbb R^m;\qquad (\mathrm P)\quad h	ext{ is polyhedral and }A(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{dom}h
e\varnothing.\]
Under \((\mathrm F)\), or under \((\mathrm S)\) with \(h\) proper, or under \((\mathrm P)\), the composite is proper and
\[\partial(h\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three elementary mapping structures give an exact affine chain rule. The outer function may have full domain; the linear part may be surjective; or the outer function may be polyhedral while the affine range meets its domain. In each regime every subgradient of the composite is the adjoint pullback of an outer subgradient.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Regime \((\mathrm F)\) makes the range-relative-interior test automatic because \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h)=\mathbb R^m\).
Regime \((\mathrm S)\) makes \(A(\mathbb R^n)=\mathbb R^m\), which necessarily meets the nonempty relative interior of the domain of a proper finite-dimensional convex function.
special_cases_latex: If \(A_0\) is invertible, it is surjective and \(\partial(h\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\).
For a coordinate projection with full-row rank, the surjective regime applies.
Every finite convex outer function belongs to regime \((\mathrm F)\), regardless of whether \(A_0\) is injective or surjective.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under surjectivity, \(A_0^*\) is injective, so the representing outer subgradient is unique whenever a composite subgradient is fixed.
For a differentiable outer function, all three regimes reduce to the classical adjoint gradient formula.
boundary_notes: Injectivity without surjectivity is not listed as an exactness mechanism for an extended-valued outer function.
The polyhedral regime still requires feasibility of the composite.
These are sufficient structural regimes, not an exhaustive characterization of exactness.

children.top_down_role: Exactness boundaries governed by mapping range and effective-domain geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Range–effective-domain boundary for affine exactness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex and let \(A(x)=A_0x+b\). Put \(R=b+\operatorname{ran}A_0\) and \(D=\operatorname{dom}h\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-valued affine composition. The boundary is geometric: it compares the affine range with the relative interior and boundary of the outer effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine chain-rule exactness boundary is the trichotomy
\[R\cap\operatorname{ri}D
e\varnothing\quad	ext{(qualified exact region)},\]
\[R\cap D
e\varnothing\ 	ext{ and }\ R\cap\operatorname{ri}D=\varnothing\quad	ext{(boundary-only feasible region)},\]
\[R\cap D=\varnothing\quad	ext{(infeasible region)}.\]
In the qualified exact region,
\[\partial(h\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\quad orall x.\]
In every region the forward inclusion \(A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\subseteq\partial(h\circ A)(x)\) remains valid wherever the composite is finite, but the cited general rule does not guarantee the reverse inclusion in the boundary-only region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exactness boundary is determined by how the affine range meets the effective domain of the outer function. Meeting its relative interior is the qualified region and guarantees the exact adjoint chain rule. Meeting only the relative boundary leaves the composite feasible but does not guarantee that every composite subgradient has an outer multiplier representation. Missing the domain makes the composite improper.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The qualified region is equivalently \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(D-R)\).
At a finite point \(x\), exactness is the multiplier-surjectivity statement \(\partial(h\circ A)(x)\subseteq A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\), since the reverse inclusion is automatic.
special_cases_latex: If \(D=\mathbb R^m\), every affine range lies in the qualified region.
If \(h\) is polyhedral, boundary-only feasibility is still sufficient for exactness by the polyhedral alternative.
If \(R\cap D=\varnothing\), then \(h(Ax)=+\infty\) for all \(x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The obstruction to exactness is not nonlinearity of the inner map but failure of transversal contact between its range and the outer domain.
The boundary identifies when multiplier representations require a separate closedness or polyhedral argument.
boundary_notes: The boundary-only regime does not assert failure of exactness; it states that relative-interior exactness is unavailable.
Range geometry concerns the entire affine range, not only the value \(Ax\) at one point.
Infinite-dimensional analogues replace relative interior by stronger generalized-interior or closedness conditions.

children.title: Closed-Range Regimes
children.top_down_role: Chain-rule exactness associated with closed mapping ranges.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(K\subset Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-image exactness criterion for the support-function model of affine chain rules.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Pre-Composition with an Affine Mapping p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms II: Advanced Theory and Bundle Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support-function composition satisfies
\[
\sigma_K(Ax)=\sigma_{A^*K}(x)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\partial(\sigma_K\circ A)(0)=\operatorname{cl}(A^*K).
\]
Since \(\partial\sigma_K(0)=K\), the ordinary chain-rule expression is \(A^*\partial\sigma_K(0)=A^*K\). Therefore the chain rule is exact at \(0\) whenever \(A^*K\) is closed, and in this model closedness is also necessary for exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a support-function composition, the subdifferential at zero is the closure of the adjoint image. The ordinary chain rule is exact precisely when that image is closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Range Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the affine space reached by \(T\) meets the relative interior of the effective domain,
\[
(b+\operatorname{ran}A)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\ne\varnothing,
\]
then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}(f\circ T)\),
\[
\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial f(Ax+b).
\]
Thus domain compatibility eliminates the possible closure or approximation defect in the reverse chain-rule inclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\), one has \(A^*M=(a,b)\), and hence
\[
A^*K=\bigl\{(a,b):a>0,\ b\in\mathbb{R}\bigr\}\cup\{(0,0)\},
\]
which is not closed. Since \(\partial\sigma_K(0)=K\),
\[
A^*\partial f(0)=A^*K
\subsetneq
\operatorname{cl}(A^*K)=\{(a,b):a\ge0,\ b\in\mathbb{R}\}
=
\partial(f\circ A)(0).
\]
Thus the unclosed chain-rule image can be strictly smaller than the true subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite-cone support function and a two-dimensional linear map produce a nonclosed adjoint image, making the ordinary affine chain-rule inclusion strict at zero.

\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact subdifferential of an increasing convex scalar composition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex and let \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex and nondecreasing. Define \(h=g\circ f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional and finite-valued. Monotonicity of the scalar outer function preserves convexity and forces its subgradients to be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A monotone scalar composition is a function
\[h(x)=g(f(x))\]
with \(f\) convex and \(g\) convex nondecreasing. Its exact subdifferential is
\[\partial h(x)= igcup_{ho\in\partial g(f(x))}ho\,\partial f(x)=\{ho s:ho\in\partial g(f(x)),\ s\in\partial f(x)\}.\]
Since \(g\) is nondecreasing, \(\partial g(f(x))\subseteq\mathbb R_+\). The convention \(0\,\partial f(x)=\{0\}\) applies in the finite-valued regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone scalar composition applies a finite convex nondecreasing scalar function to a finite convex inner function. Its subdifferential consists of all products of an outer scalar subgradient and an inner vector subgradient. Every outer scalar subgradient is nonnegative, which is the order property needed to preserve the inner convex subgradient inequalities.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\partial(g\circ f)(x)=\bigcup_{\rho\in\partial g(f(x))}\rho\partial f(x).\]
If \(g\) is differentiable at \(f(x)\), then \(\partial(g\circ f)(x)=g'(f(x))\partial f(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(g(t)=t_+=\max\{t,0\}\), the rule gives \(\partial(f_+)(x)=\partial f(x)\) when \(f(x)>0\), \(\{0\}\) when \(f(x)<0\), and \([0,1]\partial f(x)\) when \(f(x)=0\).
For differentiable \(f\), \(\partial(g\circ f)(x)=\{\rho\nabla f(x):\rho\in\partial g(f(x))\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If both functions are differentiable at the relevant points, \(\nabla(g\circ f)(x)=g'(f(x))\nabla f(x)\).
If \(0\in\partial g(f(x))\), then \(0\in\partial(g\circ f)(x)\).
boundary_notes: If \(g\) is convex but decreasing on part of the range of \(f\), the composite need not be convex.
Extended-valued functions require additional domain qualifications.
The union over \(\rho\) need not reduce to one scaled set unless the outer subdifferential is a singleton.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential chain rule for increasing scalar convex composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar convex-composition rule under the stated relative-interior range-domain qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and convex, and let \(\phi\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R)\) be increasing on \(\operatorname{ran}f\). Suppose that \[\bigl(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{ran}f)+\mathbb R_{++}\bigr)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\phi)\neq\varnothing.\] If \(\bar x\in\mathcal H\) and \(f(\bar x)\in\operatorname{dom}\phi\), then \[\partial(\phi\circ f)(\bar x)=\{\alpha u\mid (\alpha,u)\in\partial\phi(f(\bar x))\times\partial f(\bar x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous real-valued convex inner function and a proper lower-semicontinuous convex outer function that is increasing on the inner function's range, the stated relative-interior qualification yields an exact product-form subdifferential chain rule.

children.title: Cone-Monotone Vector Composition
children.top_down_role: Vector-valued convex mappings organized through cone monotonicity.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a closed convex cone, and \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is \(K\)-convex and continuous near \(\bar x\).
\(h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper convex, \(K\)-nondecreasing, and continuous at \(F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(h\circ F)(\bar x)=\bigcup_{y^*\in\partial h(F(\bar x))}\partial\langle y^*,F\rangle(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Order defined by the cone K
Scalarization mapping x to the dual pairing of y-star and F(x)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cone-ordered chain rule with continuity qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(a\preceq_K b\) by \(b-a\in K\), and suppose \(F\) is \(K\)-convex. Since \(h\) is \(K\)-nondecreasing, every \(y^*\in\partial h(F(\bar x))\) belongs to \(K^*\), so \(x\mapsto\langle y^*,F(x)\rangle\) is convex. Under the stated continuity assumptions,
\[
\partial(h\circ F)(\bar x)=\bigcup_{y^*\in\partial h(F(\bar x))}\partial\langle y^*,F\rangle(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradients of a cone-monotone vector composition are exactly subgradients of scalarizations generated by outer subgradients.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-orthant cone-monotone vector composition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), let \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) have finite convex components, and let \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex and \(K\)-nondecreasing: \(y-z\in K\Rightarrow g(y)\ge g(z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finite-valued vector composition ordered by the positive orthant. This is the sourced cone-monotone specialization; arbitrary ordering cones require a corresponding dual-cone formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone-monotone vector composition is
\[h(x)=g(F(x))=g(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x)).\]
Its outer subgradients satisfy \(\partial g(F(x))\subseteq K^*=\mathbb R_+^m\), and its exact subdifferential is
\[\partial h(x)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^mho_i s_i:ho\in\partial g(F(x)),\ s_i\in\partial f_i(x)ight\}.\]
Equivalently,
\[\partial h(x)= igcup_{ho\in\partial g(F(x))}\sum_{i=1}^mho_i\partial f_i(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-orthant cone-monotone vector composition applies a componentwise nondecreasing finite convex outer function to a vector of finite convex component functions. Outer subgradients lie in the dual ordering cone, so their coordinates are nonnegative. The composite subdifferential is the union, over all outer subgradients, of the corresponding nonnegative weighted Minkowski sums of the component subdifferentials.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A vector \(u\) is in \(\partial(g\circ F)(x)\) exactly when there are \(\rho\in\partial g(F(x))\) and \(s_i\in\partial f_i(x)\) with \(u=\sum_i\rho_i s_i\).
The order condition is \(g(z+k)\ge g(z)\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(k\in K\).
special_cases_latex: For \(g(y)=\max_i y_i\), the weights form a simplex supported on the active coordinates.
For \(g(y)=\sum_i y_i\), the only outer subgradient is \((1,\ldots,1)\), yielding the finite sum rule.
For \(m=1\), the rule is monotone scalar composition.
immediate_consequences_latex: If all functions are differentiable, \(\nabla(g\circ F)(x)=\sum_i\partial_i g(F(x))\nabla f_i(x)\).
Nondifferentiability of the outer function is represented by the choice of a weight vector in \(\partial g(F(x))\).
boundary_notes: The stated order cone is \(\mathbb R_+^m\); no unsupported arbitrary-cone chain rule is asserted.
Finite-valuedness ensures the compact subdifferentials used in the exact formula.
Without cone monotonicity, negative outer weights can invalidate convexity of the composition.

notation.meaning: Dual cone of the ordering cone; here K*=R⁺ᵐ.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active and nearby-active calculus for convex suprema
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\) be an index set, let \(f_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and assume \(f(x)=\sup_{j\in J}f_j(x)<+\infty\) for every \(x\). Define \(J(x)=\{j:f_j(x)=f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finite-valued suprema. The calculus distinguishes the unconditional active inclusion, compact-index exactness, and qualification-free recovery by nearby points and almost-active indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Extremum subdifferential calculus is organized by
\[\overline{\operatorname{co}}\! igcup_{j\in J(x)}\partial f_j(x)\subseteq\partial f(x).\]
If \(J\) is compact and \(j\mapsto f_j(y)\) is upper semicontinuous for every \(y\), then
\[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\! igcup_{j\in J(x)}\partial f_j(x).\]
Without these assumptions, define \(J_\delta(x_0)=\{j:f_j(x_0)\ge f(x_0)-\delta\}\) and
\[S_\delta= igcup_{\substack{j\in J_\delta(x_0)\\|x-x_0\|\le\delta}}\partial f_j(x).\]
Then the general recovery formula is
\[\partial f(x_0)= igcap_{\delta>0}\overline{\operatorname{co}}S_\delta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extremum subdifferential calculus uses active indices for exact compactly indexed suprema and nearby almost-active indices for general suprema. Active component subgradients always generate a subset of the supremum subdifferential. Compactness and upper semicontinuity make the active convex hull exact. Without them, exact recovery requires closed convex hulls of subgradients evaluated both at almost-active indices and at nearby points, followed by intersection as the tolerance tends to zero.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under compact-index upper-semicontinuity, nearby almost-active recovery collapses to the convex hull of subdifferentials at exactly active indices.
The unconditional inclusion means every active component subgradient is a subgradient of the supremum.
special_cases_latex: For finite \(J\), compactness and upper semicontinuity are automatic, giving the finite-maximum rule.
If all active \(f_j\) are differentiable, the exact compact-index formula is the convex hull of their active gradients.
immediate_consequences_latex: Almost-active indices repair the possibility that \(J(x_0)\) is empty.
Nearby evaluation repairs examples where all subdifferentials at \(x_0\) are too small to generate \(\partial f(x_0)\).
boundary_notes: Almost-active indices alone are insufficient in the fully general formula; nearby points are also required.
Closure cannot generally be removed from the qualification-free recovery formula.
The supremum is assumed finite-valued on all of \(\mathbb R^n\) in the cited general result.

notation.meaning: Union of component subdifferentials at nearby points for delta-active indices.

children.title: Finite Maximum Rules
children.top_down_role: Active-piece and convex-hull organization for finite maxima.

assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is finite and continuous at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(\bar x)=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I(\bar x)}\partial f_i(\bar x)\bigr)\).

notation.meaning: Indices attaining the maximum at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional rule for a finite maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\) and \(I(\bar x)=\{i:f_i(\bar x)=f(\bar x)\}\). Then only active functions contribute, and the exact maximum rule is
\[
\partial f(\bar x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(\bar x)}\partial f_i(\bar x)\right).
\]
Equivalently, every subgradient is a convex combination of subgradients selected from active pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite maximum is the convex hull of the subdifferentials of the active functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Maximum Rules

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The active-piece convex-hull formula is standard and appropriately classified as a representation, but the record supplies no inspectable source with a section, theorem, or page locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-piece convex-hull rule for a finite maximum
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex functions and define \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\). The active index set is \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finite maxima of finite-valued convex functions. The active set is nonempty and finite, so no closure or approximate-activity construction is needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite maximum rule is
\[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\!\left( igcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)ight).\]
Equivalently, \(u\in\partial f(x)\) exactly when there exist coefficients \(\lambda_i\ge0\) and vectors \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\), indexed by \(i\in I(x)\), such that
\[\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1,\qquad u=\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i u_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the pointwise maximum of finitely many finite convex functions, the subdifferential at a point is the convex hull of the subdifferentials of precisely the active functions. Thus every subgradient of the maximum is a convex combination of subgradients chosen from active pieces, and every such convex combination is a subgradient of the maximum.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\partial f(x)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i u_i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1,\ u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\right\}.\]
The rule is the monotone-vector composition formula for \(g(y)=\max_i y_i\), whose subdifferential is the simplex supported on active coordinates.
special_cases_latex: If \(I(x)=\{k\}\), then \(\partial f(x)=\partial f_k(x)\).
If every active function is differentiable at \(x\), then \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\).
For affine pieces \(f_i(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\), \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The condition \(0\in\partial f(x)\) is equivalent to the existence of active subgradients whose convex combination is zero.
If exactly one piece is active and differentiable, the maximum is differentiable at that point with the same gradient.
boundary_notes: Inactive functions contribute no subgradients to the formula.
The finite-valued hypothesis avoids additional domain-normal terms.
For infinite index sets, compactness, upper semicontinuity, closure, or nearby almost-active constructions may be necessary.

children.title: Compact-Index Supremum Rules
children.top_down_role: Supremum calculus supported by compactness and active-index stability.

assumptions_latex: \(T\) is compact and each \(f_t:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
The mapping \((x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)\) is jointly continuous on \(U\times T\) for a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(\bar x)=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\bigcup_{t\in T(\bar x)}\partial f_t(\bar x)\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-index exact supremum rule under joint continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\sup_{t\in T}f_t(x)\). Compactness and joint continuity ensure that the supremum is attained locally and that \(T(\bar x)=\{t\in T:f_t(\bar x)=f(\bar x)\}\) is nonempty and compact. The subdifferential is
\[
\partial f(\bar x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{t\in T(\bar x)}\partial f_t(\bar x)\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a jointly continuous compact family, the supremum subdifferential is the convex hull of active component subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Index Supremum Rules

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed active-index representation matches the terminal container, but an authoritative source is needed to confirm that compactness and the stated joint continuity alone yield the exact formula without an additional closure or qualification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact-index supremum subdifferential rule
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\) be a compact metric space and let \(f_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(j\in J\), be finite convex functions such that \(j\mapsto f_j(y)\) is upper semicontinuous for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finite-valued convex analysis with a compact index set and pointwise upper semicontinuity in the index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the supremum function and its active-index set by \[f(y):=\sup_{j\in J}f_j(y),\qquad J(x):=\{j\in J:f_j(x)=f(x)\}.\] The compact-index supremum rule is the identity \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\!\left(\bigcup_{j\in J(x)}\partial f_j(x)\right).\] Compactness and upper semicontinuity ensure that \(J(x)\) is nonempty and compact. If every \(f_j\) is differentiable, the generating set reduces to the active gradients: \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_j(x):j\in J(x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a pointwise supremum of finite convex functions indexed by a compact metric space, with upper-semicontinuous dependence on the index, the active indices at \(x\) are those attaining the supremum. The compact-index rule identifies the subdifferential of the supremum with the convex hull of the subdifferentials of the active functions. In the differentiable case it is the convex hull of the active gradients.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For differentiable members, \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_j(x):j\in J(x)\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(J(x)=\{j_x\}\) and \(f_{j_x}\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \(\nabla f(x)=\nabla f_{j_x}(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The active set is nonempty because an upper-semicontinuous real function on compact \(J\) attains its maximum.
boundary_notes: Without compactness or upper semicontinuity, the active set may be empty and active subgradients alone need not recover the full subdifferential.
The stated rule is finite-dimensional and does not assert an infinite-dimensional weak-star analogue.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradients expose a convex-function maximizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-support consequence at a relative-interior-domain maximizer over an arbitrary nonempty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper and convex, and let \(S\neq\varnothing\) be a set on which \(f\) is nonconstant. If \(x\in S\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and \(f(x)=\sup_{y\in S}f(y)\), then every \(x^*\in\partial f(x)\) is nonzero and satisfies \(\langle x,x^*\rangle=\sup_{y\in S}\langle y,x^*\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a proper convex function attains its supremum over a nonempty set at a relative-interior-domain point and is not constant on that set, every subgradient there is nonzero and defines a linear functional maximized over the set at the same point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x^*\in\partial f(x):\quad x^*\neq0\ \text{ and }\ \langle x,x^*\rangle=\sup_{y\in S}\langle y,x^*\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate-active closure calculus for arbitrary suprema
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\) be arbitrary, let \(f_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and suppose \(f:=\sup_{j\in J}f_j\) is finite on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Fix \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finite-valued convex supremum calculus without compactness or attainment of the index supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\delta>0\), define the approximately active indices and nearby subgradients by \[J_\delta(x_0):=\{j\in J:f_j(x_0)\ge f(x_0)-\delta\},\] \[S_\delta(x_0):=\bigcup\{\partial f_j(x):j\in J_\delta(x_0),\ \|x-x_0\|\le\delta\}.\] The general supremum closure object at \(x_0\) is \[\mathcal G(x_0):=\bigcap_{\delta>0}\overline{\operatorname{co}}S_\delta(x_0).\] General supremum closure calculus identifies this object with the convex subdifferential: \[\partial f(x_0)=\mathcal G(x_0).\] Thus approximate activity, nearby base points, convexification, closure, and intersection over all tolerances replace an exact active-index formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a general index family, exact maximizers may not exist. At each tolerance \(\delta\), retain indices whose value at \(x_0\) is within \(\delta\) of the supremum and collect their subgradients at points within distance \(\delta\) of \(x_0\). The closed convex hulls of these sets form a decreasing family, and their intersection is the subdifferential of the supremum.
equivalent_formulations_latex: It suffices to intersect along any sequence \(\delta_k\downarrow0\): \(\partial f(x_0)=\bigcap_k\overline{\operatorname{co}}S_{\delta_k}(x_0)\).
special_cases_latex: When the compact-index hypotheses make exact active indices stable, the construction collapses to the convex hull of active subdifferentials.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exact active subgradient belongs to each sufficiently enlarged approximate-active construction.
boundary_notes: Dropping the nearby-point component can lose limiting subgradients.
The formula assumes the supremum is finite-valued; extended-valued variants require additional domain qualifications.

children.title: Approximate Active Indices
children.top_down_role: Near-active index structures used when exact activity is insufficient.

assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\sup_{t\in T}f_t(x)\) is finite at the point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate activity for arbitrary supremum families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a family \((f_t)_{t\in T}\) with \(f(x)=\sup_{t\in T}f_t(x)<+\infty\), the set of \(\varepsilon\)-active indices at \(x\) is
\[
T_\varepsilon(x):=\{t\in T:f_t(x)\ge f(x)-\varepsilon\}.
\]
Thus \(T_0(x)\) is the exact active set, while \(T_\varepsilon(x)\) may be nonempty even when the supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An index is epsilon-active when its value lies within epsilon of the supremum at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Active Indices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise, internally consistent, and correctly placed, but the record contains neither a citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale satisfying the evidence contract.

children.title: Closed Convex-Hull Recovery
children.top_down_role: Closure structures needed to recover general supremum subgradients.

assumptions_latex: \(f=\sup_{t\in T}f_t\) is proper convex and finite and continuous at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional recovery using approximate activity and closed convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(T_\varepsilon(\bar x)=\{t:f_t(\bar x)\ge f(\bar x)-\varepsilon\}\), the general supremum formula is
\[
\partial f(\bar x)=\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\!\left(\bigcup_{t\in T_\varepsilon(\bar x)}\partial_\varepsilon f_t(\bar x)\right).
\]
The intersection removes the approximation error, while closure and convexification retain limiting mixtures of subgradients whose indices need not be exactly active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general supremum subdifferential is recovered by intersecting closed convex hulls of epsilon-subgradients from epsilon-active functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex-Hull Recovery

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation belongs in the closed convex-hull recovery container, but the exact use of the same epsilon for activity and approximate subdifferentials, together with the stated hypotheses, requires authoritative source validation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-section subgradients of a general supremum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States only the one-sided relative-subdifferential inclusion; it does not assert equality or attainment of an active index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Delta\ne\varnothing, let Q be a nonempty convex subset of a real finite-dimensional vector space, and suppose \phi(\cdot,y):Q\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} is closed and convex for every y\in\Delta. Define f(x)=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y), \hat Q=\{x\in Q:f(x)<+\infty\}, and I(x)=\{y\in\Delta:\phi(x,y)=f(x)\}. Then f is convex on \hat Q and closed as an extended-real-valued function on \hat Q. For every x\in\hat Q, \partial_{\hat Q}f(x)\supseteq\operatorname{Conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{y\in I(x)}\partial_{Q,x}\phi(x,y)\right).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of an arbitrary nonempty family of closed convex sections is closed and convex on its finite-value domain. At each point of that domain, the relative subdifferential contains the convex hull of the relative subdifferentials of all active sections; only inclusion is asserted.
assumptions_latex: Q\ne\varnothing\text{ is convex in a real finite-dimensional vector space}
\phi(\cdot,y)\text{ is closed and convex on }Q\text{ for every }y\in\Delta
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex and closed on }\hat Q,\quad \partial_{\hat Q}f(x)\supseteq\operatorname{Conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{y\in I(x)}\partial_{Q,x}\phi(x,y)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine precomposition of a closed convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the bounded-domain restriction and the nonempty-subdifferential condition stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be closed and convex, let \varnothing\ne S\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f be bounded with f convex and finite on S, and let \mathcal{A}(x)=Ax+b. Define \phi(x)=f(\mathcal{A}(x)) and Q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\mathcal{A}(x)\in S\}. Then \phi is convex on Q and closed as an extended-real-valued function. For every x\in Q satisfying \partial f(\mathcal{A}(x))\ne\varnothing, \partial\phi(x)=A^T\partial f(\mathcal{A}(x)).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex function composed with an affine map, the resulting function is closed and is convex on the stated inverse-image set. At every point of that set where the original subdifferential is nonempty, the composite subdifferential is the transpose-linear image of the original subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne S\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\text{ is bounded, and }f\text{ is convex and finite on }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi=f\circ\mathcal{A}\text{ is convex on }Q\text{ and closed, and }\partial\phi(x)=A^T\partial f(\mathcal{A}(x)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of a sum of absolute linear forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formula separates positive, negative, and zero inner-product indices and interprets the last sum as a Minkowski sum of line segments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^n and f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m|\langle a_i,x\rangle|. For x\in\mathbb{R}^n, define I_-(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle<0\}, I_+(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle>0\}, and I_0(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle=0\}. Then \partial f(x)=\sum_{i\in I_+(x)}a_i-\sum_{i\in I_-(x)}a_i+\sum_{i\in I_0(x)}[-a_i,a_i], where [-a_i,a_i]=\{ta_i:t\in[-1,1]\} and the set sum is Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite sum of absolute linear forms, each positive inner product contributes its vector, each negative inner product contributes the negative vector, and each zero inner product contributes the entire line segment between the two; the zero-index contributions are combined by Minkowski addition.
assumptions_latex: I_-(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle<0\},\quad I_+(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle>0\},\quad I_0(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle=0\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of a nonnegative weighted sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retains nonnegative weights, including the stated zero-weight boundary, and restricts the formula to the interior of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be closed convex functions and let \alpha_1,\alpha_2\ge0. For f=\alpha_1f_1+\alpha_2f_2, the function f is closed and convex, \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_1)\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_2), and, for every x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f), \partial f(x)=\alpha_1\partial f_1(x)+\alpha_2\partial f_2(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative weighted sum of two closed convex functions is closed and convex. Its domain interior is the intersection of the two domain interiors, and at every point in that interior its subdifferential is the Minkowski sum of the correspondingly weighted subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and convex},\quad \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\bigcap_{i=1}^2\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_i),\quad \partial f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^2\alpha_i\partial f_i(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of a finite maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to finitely many extended-real closed convex functions and points in the interior of the maximum's effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}, i=1,\ldots,m, be closed and convex, and set f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x). Then f is closed and convex and \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_i). For every x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f), if I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}, then \partial f(x)=\operatorname{Conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite maximum of closed convex functions is closed and convex, with domain interior equal to the intersection of the component domain interiors. At an interior point, its subdifferential is the convex hull of the subdifferentials of the active component functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and convex},\quad \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_i),\quad \partial f(x)=\operatorname{Conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of exact activity without compactness or attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
f(x)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left(x-\frac1n\right)=x,
\]
but no finite index attains the supremum. Hence \(T(x)=\varnothing\), whereas \(\partial f(x)=\{1\}\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{n\in T(x)}\partial f_n(x)\right)=\varnothing\ne\partial f(x).
\]
Approximate active indices are therefore indispensable in this noncompact regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noncompact affine family can have no active index even though its supremum has a nonempty subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of the Coordinatewise Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact formula at an arbitrary point, including the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be given by f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le n}x^{(i)}, and let I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x^{(i)}=f(x)\}. Then, for every x\in\mathbb{R}^n, \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{e_i:i\in I(x)\}. In particular, \partial f(0)=\operatorname{conv}\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}=\Delta_n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the maximum of the coordinates, the subdifferential at a point is the convex hull of the standard basis vectors corresponding to coordinates attaining the maximum. At the origin it is the standard simplex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex marginal function and minimizing-fiber calculus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(g:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex partial minimization; lower semicontinuity and attainment are recorded separately rather than inferred from convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The marginal function, minimizing fiber, and approximate minimizing fiber are \[p(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}g(x,y),\qquad M(x):=\{y:g(x,y)=p(x)\},\] \[M_\varepsilon(x):=\{y:g(x,y)\le p(x)+\varepsilon\}\quad(\varepsilon>0).\] Equivalently, with the projection \(A:X\times Y\to X\), \(A(x,y)=x\), the marginal is the infimal image \[(Ag)(x):=\inf\{g(z):Az=x\}=p(x).\] Whenever \(p(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\), joint convexity makes \(p\) convex. The associated exact attained-fiber subgradient object is \[\{u\in X:(u,0)\in\partial g(x,y)\},\qquad y\in M(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal-marginal calculus begins with a jointly convex extended-real function and eliminates the second variable by taking an infimum. It records the value function \(p\), the exact minimizer set \(M\), and the approximate minimizer sets \(M_\varepsilon\). The same operation is the infimal image of \(g\) under the coordinate projection. At an attained fiber, marginal subgradients are represented by joint subgradients whose eliminated-coordinate component is zero.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The strict epigraph of \(p\) is the projection of the strict epigraph of \(g\) onto \(X\times\mathbb{R}\).
special_cases_latex: Infimal convolution is obtained from \(g(x,y)=f_1(y)+f_2(x-y)\).
Linear elimination is obtained by replacing the coordinate projection with a general surjective linear map.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(g\) is jointly convex and the marginal never equals \(-\infty\), then \(p\) is convex.
boundary_notes: Joint convexity does not by itself guarantee that \(p\) is lower semicontinuous or that \(M(x)\) is nonempty.
The exact subgradient representation requires an attained minimizing fiber.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimizer-indexed Danskin subgradient family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Y\) be a compact metric space and \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^n\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy: \(x\mapsto\phi(x,y)\) is finite convex for every \(y\), and \(y\mapsto\phi(x,y)\) is upper semicontinuous for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex maximization value functions with compact parameter sets; the differentiable specialization uses gradients with respect to the decision variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the value function and optimizer set by \[V(x):=\max_{y\in Y}\phi(x,y),\qquad Y(x):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}\phi(x,y).\] The Danskin subgradient family at \(x\) is \[\mathcal D(x):=\operatorname{co}\!\left(\bigcup_{y\in Y(x)}\partial_x\phi(x,y)\right).\] Under the stated compactness and semicontinuity hypotheses, \(Y(x)\neq\varnothing\), and the associated value-function rule is \[\partial V(x)=\mathcal D(x).\] If every \(x\mapsto\phi(x,y)\) is differentiable, then \(\mathcal D(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla_x\phi(x,y):y\in Y(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Danskin family consists of a maximum value function, its set of maximizing parameters, and the convex hull of the decision-variable subgradients selected at those maximizers. Compactness and upper semicontinuity give an attained optimizer set, and the family equals the convex subdifferential of the value function. For smooth parameterized functions, only the gradients at maximizing parameters are needed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In the differentiable case, \(\partial V(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla_x\phi(x,y):y\in Y(x)\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(Y(x)=\{y(x)\}\) and \(\phi(\cdot,y(x))\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(\nabla V(x)=\nabla_x\phi(x,y(x))\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Multiple maximizers generate a convex set of possible value-function subgradients.
boundary_notes: This record uses a maximizing value function; minimizing value functions require joint-convex marginal calculus rather than a sign change without further hypotheses.
Uniqueness of an optimizer is sufficient for the displayed smooth specialization but is not part of the general definition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex marginal rule when the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\bar y\in Y(\bar x)\). Attainment gives \(F(\bar x,\bar y)=p(\bar x)\), and the exact marginal relation is
\[
u\in\partial p(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (u,0)\in\partial F(\bar x,\bar y).
\]
This equivalence holds for every \(\bar y\in Y(\bar x)\); thus the projected subgradient description is independent of which minimizing selection is chosen.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At any attained minimizer, value-function subgradients are exactly joint subgradients whose optimizer-coordinate component is zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attained optimizer-selection regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}\phi(x,y)\), where each \(\phi(\cdot,y)\) is finite convex, and fix \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise attained convex maximum-value functions; compactness is one sufficient mechanism for attainment but is not built into the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The value function is in an attained regime at \(x\) when \[Y(x):=\{y\in Y:\phi(x,y)=V(x)\}\neq\varnothing.\] Its active selection graph and selected-subgradient set are \[\operatorname{gph}Y:=\{(x,y):y\in Y(x)\},\qquad G(x):=\bigcup_{y\in Y(x)}\partial_x\phi(x,y).\] An attained exact-selection regime is one for which the value-function subdifferential is generated without limiting approximate optimizers: \[\partial V(x)=\operatorname{co}G(x).\] For a minimizing marginal \(p(x)=\inf_y g(x,y)\), the analogous attained condition is \(M(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_y g(x,y)\neq\varnothing\), with selected joint subgradients satisfying \((u,0)\in\partial g(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained value-function regime is a point where the supremum or infimum defining the value is realized by at least one parameter. The optimizer mapping, its graph, and the subgradients selected from exact optimizers are explicit objects. In an exact-selection regime these selected subgradients, after convexification for a maximum value function, generate the full value-function subdifferential without closure over approximate optimizers.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Attainment means that the optimal value belongs to \(\{\phi(x,y):y\in Y\}\), rather than merely to its closure.
special_cases_latex: A compact parameter set with upper-semicontinuous parameter dependence yields attainment.
A singleton optimizer set gives a single selected subdifferential.
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact optimizer selections can be used directly in the active subgradient formula.
boundary_notes: Attainment alone does not guarantee the exact subdifferential identity; the appropriate compactness, semicontinuity, or marginal hypotheses remain necessary.
Nonattained values require approximate-selection closure objects.
