knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearby exact-subgradient approximation relation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\varepsilon\geq0\), define \(\partial_\varepsilon f(x)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle s,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean formulation of the Brøndsted–Rockafellar approximation relation, with simultaneous perturbation of the base point and subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\eta>0\), define the nearby exact-subgradient relation by \[\mathcal R_{f,\varepsilon,\eta}(x,s)=\{(x_\eta,s_\eta)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\mid \|x_\eta-x\|\leq\eta,\ \|s_\eta-s\|\leq\varepsilon/\eta\}.\] Whenever \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(s\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\), and \(\eta>0\), this set is nonempty. Thus approximate subgradient information at \(x\) is converted into an exact graph point while controlling both perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every point \(x\), every \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient \(s\) at \(x\), and every radius \(\eta>0\), the nearby exact-subgradient relation consists of exact graph points \((x_\eta,s_\eta)\) satisfying \(\|x_\eta-x\|\leq\eta\) and \(\|s_\eta-s\|\leq\varepsilon/\eta\); this relation is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\subseteq\displaystyle\bigcup_{\|y-x\|\leq\eta}\bigl(\partial f(y)+B(0,\varepsilon/\eta)\bigr)\) for every \(\eta>0\).
special_cases_latex: Choosing \(\eta=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) for \(\varepsilon>0\) gives \(\|x_\eta-x\|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) and \(\|s_\eta-s\|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\).
If \(\varepsilon=0\), one may take \((x_\eta,s_\eta)=(x,s)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient lies within \(\varepsilon/\eta\) of an exact subgradient evaluated at a point within \(\eta\) of its original base point.
boundary_notes: The displayed quantitative statement uses the Euclidean norm and does not assert the most general Banach-space version.
Neither closeness estimate alone guarantees that the exact subgradient occurs at the original base point.

notation.meaning: set of nearby exact graph points satisfying the two error bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the enlarged graph \(G_\varepsilon(f)=\{(x,s)\mid x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ s\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\}\) and the exact graph \(G_0(f)=\operatorname{gra}\partial f\). For every \(\varepsilon\geq0\), \[G_\varepsilon(f)\subseteq G_0(f)+B_\infty(0,\sqrt{\varepsilon})\] when \(\varepsilon>0\), with equality of the error radius to zero when \(\varepsilon=0\). Consequently, if \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\) and \((x_k,s_k)\in G_{\varepsilon_k}(f)\), exact points can be selected whose product-norm distance from \((x_k,s_k)\) tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The enlarged graph \(G_\varepsilon(f)\) contains all base-point and epsilon-subgradient pairs. Every such pair is within product-norm distance \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) of the exact subdifferential graph. Hence enlarged graph points with approximation levels tending to zero admit asymptotically coincident exact graph points.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(\varepsilon\geq0\), and \(G_\varepsilon(f)\) is defined using the global convex epsilon-subdifferential.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \((x,s)\in G_\varepsilon(f)\), there is \((y,t)\in G_0(f)\) with \(\|y-x\|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) and \(\|t-s\|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\).
\(\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\sup_{z\in G_\varepsilon(f)}d_\infty(z,G_0(f))=0\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\varepsilon=0\), \(G_\varepsilon(f)=G_0(f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{ran}\partial f}\) for every fixed \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
Vanishing enlargement error controls both the primal and dual coordinates of a nearby exact graph point.
boundary_notes: The inclusion is one-sided: arbitrary points near \(G_0(f)\) need not belong to \(G_\varepsilon(f)\).
For fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), the enlarged graph need not equal the closure of the exact graph.

For every \((x,x^*)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial_\varepsilon f\) and every \(\lambda>0\), there exists \((\bar x,\bar x^*)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\) such that

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a real Banach space \(X\), the approximation bounds are measured in \(X\) and \(X^*\): there exist \(\bar x\in X\) and \(\bar x^*\in\partial f(\bar x)\) such that
\[
\|\bar x-x\|\leq\lambda,
\qquad
\|\bar x^*-x^*\|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}.
\]
If \(X=H\) is a real Hilbert space, the Riesz identification \(H\simeq H^*\) expresses both bounds in the Hilbert norm. If \(X=\mathbb{R}^d\) with the Euclidean norm, the same bounds hold under \(\mathbb{R}^d\simeq(\mathbb{R}^d)^*\), without a dimension-dependent constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Banach-space approximation bounds specialize to Hilbert and Euclidean spaces through their standard dual identifications, without introducing a dimension-dependent constant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Space-indexed exact-subgradient approximation property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real normed space with continuous dual \(X^*\), dual pairing \(\langle x^*,x\rangle\), and dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\). Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the common quantitative approximation template and distinguishes Euclidean, Hilbert, and Banach ambient regimes without identifying their dual spaces unless justified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The space \(X\) is said to satisfy the quantitative exact-subgradient approximation property \(\mathrm{BR}(X)\) if, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(x^*\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\), and \(\lambda,\mu\geq0\) with \(\varepsilon\leq\lambda\mu\), there exists \((z,z^*)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\) such that \(\|z-x\|\leq\lambda\) and \(\|z^*-x^*\|_*\leq\mu\). The Euclidean regime is \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\); the Hilbert regime identifies \(X^*\) with \(X\) by the Riesz map; the Banach regime retains distinct primal and dual coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The property \(\mathrm{BR}(X)\) means that every epsilon-subgradient pair can be replaced by an exact subdifferential graph point whose primal error is at most \(\lambda\) and dual error at most \(\mu\), provided \(\varepsilon\leq\lambda\mu\). Euclidean, Hilbert, and Banach regimes differ in their ambient geometry and in whether primal and dual spaces are canonically identified.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed space and \(X^*\) is its continuous dual.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{BR}(X)\) is the quantified existence condition \(\exists(z,z^*)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f:\ \|z-x\|\leq\lambda,\ \|z^*-x^*\|_*\leq\mu\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: In a Hilbert space, \(x^*\) and \(z^*\) may be represented by vectors in the same space, so both estimates use the Hilbert norm.
In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), setting \(\lambda=\eta\) and \(\mu=\varepsilon/\eta\) recovers the standard Euclidean formulation for \(\eta>0\).
special_cases_latex: The Hilbert-space theorem applies to \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) through the Fenchel–Young gap condition \(f(x)+f^*(x^*)\leq\langle x,x^*\rangle+\lambda\mu\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Choosing balanced tolerances \(\lambda=\mu=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) yields symmetric primal-dual error bounds whenever the norms are comparably normalized.
boundary_notes: The cited sources directly support the Euclidean and Hilbert regimes; this record does not assert an unrestricted Banach-space theorem.
In a general Banach space, writing both coordinates in \(X\) would erase the essential distinction between \(X\) and \(X^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex subdifferential operator structure
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. The graph of a set-valued operator \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is \(\operatorname{gra}A=\{(x,u)\mid u\in Ax\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic monotone and cyclically monotone structure of convex subdifferentials; general splitting algorithms are outside this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subdifferential operator associated with \(f\) is \[\partial f:x\mapsto\{u\in\mathcal H\mid f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\ \forall y\in\mathcal H\}.\] It is regarded as a monotone operator because every \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\) satisfy \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\). More strongly, for every finite cycle \((x_i,u_i)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\), with \(x_{m+1}=x_1\), one has \(\sum_{i=1}^m\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,u_i\rangle\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subdifferential is the set-valued operator assigning to each point all slopes of global affine minorants touching the function there. Its graph is pairwise monotone and, more strongly, cyclically monotone along every finite closed cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper for the definition of \(\partial f\).
The monotonicity statements concern pairs or finite cycles contained in \(\operatorname{gra}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f\) is monotone and cyclically monotone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Pairwise monotonicity is equivalent to \(\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle\geq\langle x,v\rangle+\langle y,u\rangle\) for graph points \((x,u)\) and \((y,v)\).
Cyclic monotonicity specializes to ordinary monotonicity when the cycle length is two.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at every point of its domain, the operator is single-valued there and the pairwise condition becomes \(\langle x-y,\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\rangle\geq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every convex subdifferential graph is a monotone subset of \(\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\).
boundary_notes: A monotone operator need not be a convex subdifferential; cyclic monotonicity is the additional potential structure.
Properness alone supports monotonicity and cyclic monotonicity, while maximality requires the closed-convex hypotheses used in later records.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cyclically Monotone and Maximal Cyclically Monotone Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional definitions for multivalued mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multivalued mapping \rho:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n is cyclically monotone if, for every integer m\geq 0 and every family (x_i,x_i^*)_{i=0}^m with x_i^*\in\rho(x_i), one has \sum_{i=0}^m\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,x_i^*\rangle\leq 0, where x_{m+1}=x_0. It is maximal cyclically monotone if its graph is not properly contained in the graph of any other cyclically monotone mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multivalued mapping is cyclically monotone when every finite cycle in its graph satisfies the cyclic monotonicity inequality. It is maximal cyclically monotone when its graph has no proper cyclically monotone extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho\text{ is cyclically monotone}\iff \forall m\in\mathbb{N}_0\ \forall (x_i,x_i^*)_{i=0}^m\subset\operatorname{gph}\rho,\ \sum_{i=0}^m\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,x_i^*\rangle\leq 0;\quad \rho\text{ is maximal cyclically monotone}\iff \nexists\widetilde\rho\text{ cyclically monotone with }\operatorname{gph}\rho\subsetneq\operatorname{gph}\widetilde\rho.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity and maximality hierarchy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be a set-valued operator on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pairwise, cyclic, and graph-maximal levels relevant to convex subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The hierarchy consists of four graph properties. The operator \(A\) is monotone if \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\) for all graph pairs. It is cyclically monotone if every finite graph cycle satisfies \(\sum_i\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,u_i\rangle\leq0\). It is maximally monotone if it is monotone and has no proper monotone graph extension. It is maximally cyclically monotone if it is cyclically monotone and has no proper cyclically monotone graph extension. Cyclic monotonicity implies monotonicity, but maximal cyclic monotonicity and maximal monotonicity express maximality in different admissible classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hierarchy separates pairwise monotonicity, all finite-cycle monotonicity, nonextendability among monotone graphs, and nonextendability among cyclically monotone graphs. Cyclic monotonicity is stronger than pairwise monotonicity, while each maximality notion is relative to its own graph class.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is an arbitrary set-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{CycMon}\subseteq\mathrm{Mon}\), while maximality is defined by absence of a proper extension in the corresponding class.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone exactly when every point monotonically related to \(\operatorname{gra}A\) already lies in \(\operatorname{gra}A\).
special_cases_latex: Every maximally monotone operator that is cyclically monotone is maximally cyclically monotone.
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(\partial f\) occupies both maximal levels: it is maximally monotone and maximally cyclically monotone.
boundary_notes: Maximally cyclically monotone does not mean maximal among all monotone graphs by definition alone.
There exist maximally monotone operators that are not even three-cyclically monotone.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and set \(G_f=\operatorname{gra}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise graph geometry only; cyclic and maximal extensions are treated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph \(G_f\) is a monotone subdifferential graph when \[\forall (x,u),(y,v)\in G_f,\qquad \langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0.\] Equivalently, the cross-pairing inequality \(\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle\geq\langle x,v\rangle+\langle y,u\rangle\) holds for every two graph points. This condition is intrinsic to the graph and is unchanged by adding a constant to \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subdifferential graph is monotone when the difference of any two primal coordinates has a nonnegative inner product with the difference of their subgradients. The same property can be written as a two-point cross-pairing inequality and depends only on the graph, not on the additive normalization of the convex function.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle-\langle x,v\rangle-\langle y,u\rangle\geq0\).
For every \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), \(\|x-y+\alpha(u-v)\|\geq\|x-y\|\).
special_cases_latex: If \(u=v\), the monotonicity inequality is an equality.
For \(f=\iota_C\), the condition becomes monotonicity of the normal-cone graph \(N_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: No two graph points can satisfy \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle<0\).
Translations of the function by constants preserve \(G_f\) and its monotonicity.
boundary_notes: Monotonicity does not imply that the graph is single-valued.
Pairwise monotonicity alone does not characterize subdifferential graphs in dimensions greater than one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximal-monotone convex subdifferential
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), meaning that \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space maximality of the exact convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex subdifferential \(\partial f\) is a maximal-monotone subdifferential when it is monotone and no monotone operator \(B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) has \(\operatorname{gra}\partial f\subsetneq\operatorname{gra}B\). Every \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) has this property. Equivalently, if \((x,u)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\) satisfies \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\) for all \((y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\), then \(u\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space, its subdifferential graph is monotone and cannot be enlarged while preserving monotonicity. A point monotonically related to the entire graph must already be a subgradient pair.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+\partial f)=\mathcal H\).
\((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\iff \langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\ \forall(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\iota_C\) with \(C\) nonempty, closed, and convex, the normal-cone operator \(N_C=\partial\iota_C\) is maximally monotone.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point of \(\mathcal H\) lies in the range of \(\operatorname{Id}+\partial f\).
The resolvent \((\operatorname{Id}+\partial f)^{-1}\) has full domain.
boundary_notes: Lower semicontinuity and convexity are material to this maximality statement.
Maximal monotonicity means maximality under graph inclusion, not that individual values \(\partial f(x)\) are maximal subsets of \(\mathcal H\).

children.title: Maximal Graph Structure
children.top_down_role: Nonextendability properties of convex subdifferential graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal monotonicity in the Banach-space primal–dual formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex subdifferential \(\partial f:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is monotone and admits no proper monotone extension: if \(A:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is monotone and
\[
\operatorname{gra}\partial f\subseteq\operatorname{gra}A,
\]
then
\[
\operatorname{gra}A=\operatorname{gra}\partial f.
\]
Equivalently, whenever \((x,x^*)\in X\times X^*\) is monotonically related to every point of \(\operatorname{gra}\partial f\), one has \(x^*\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function has no strictly larger monotone graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Graph Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximal-monotonicity theorem is standard and fits the maximal graph leaf, but no source record or inspectable theorem/section/page locator is supplied for the stated Banach-space version.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone-polar closure of a subdifferential graph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a subset \(G\subseteq\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\), define its monotone polar by \[G^\mu=\{(x,u)\mid \langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq0\ \forall(y,v)\in G\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-theoretic recognition of nonextendability for convex subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A monotone graph \(G\) has maximal graph structure when \(G=G^\mu\). For \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), the exact subdifferential graph has this structure: \[\operatorname{gra}\partial f=(\operatorname{gra}\partial f)^\mu.\] Thus adjoining any point outside \(\operatorname{gra}\partial f\) violates monotonicity with at least one existing graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The monotone polar of a graph consists of all points monotonically related to every graph point. A convex subdifferential graph equals its monotone polar, so every point outside it conflicts with monotonicity and cannot be adjoined to form a larger monotone graph.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There is no monotone \(B\) with \(\operatorname{gra}\partial f\subsetneq\operatorname{gra}B\).
For every \((x,u)\notin\operatorname{gra}\partial f\), there exists \((y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\) such that \(\langle x-y,u-v\rangle<0\).
special_cases_latex: If \((x,u)\) is monotonically related to \(\operatorname{gra}\partial f\), then \(u\in\partial f(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The graph is completely recoverable from its pairwise monotonicity inequalities.
Any proper graph extension necessarily ceases to be monotone.
boundary_notes: The monotone polar need not itself be monotone for an arbitrary set \(G\).
Graph maximality does not imply that the graph equals all of \(\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\).

children.top_down_role: Recognition of maximality through resolvent and range structures.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minty range and resolvent interface
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be monotone on a real Hilbert space and let \(\gamma>0\). Define \(J_{\gamma A}=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space recognition of maximal monotonicity through the shifted range and resolvent domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minty range interface is the equivalence \[A\text{ is maximally monotone}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)=\mathcal H\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{dom}J_{\gamma A}=\mathcal H.\] For \(x,p\in\mathcal H\), the resolvent relation is \[p\in J_{\gamma A}x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-p\in\gamma Ap.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone operator on a Hilbert space, maximal monotonicity is equivalent to surjectivity of the shifted operator and to the resolvent having full domain. The resolvent point \(p\) is characterized by the inclusion \(x-p\in\gamma Ap\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone if and only if \(\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)=\mathcal H\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone if and only if \(J_{\gamma A}\) is defined on all of \(\mathcal H\).
\(p\in J_{\gamma A}x\iff(p,\gamma^{-1}(x-p))\in\operatorname{gra}A\).
special_cases_latex: For \(A=\partial f\) with \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), the range condition always holds.
At \(\gamma=1\), the criterion is \(\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}+A)=\mathcal H\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The range criterion converts a graph-maximality property into a solvability condition for \(x\in p+\gamma Ap\).
boundary_notes: Monotonicity is required before surjectivity is used as a maximality criterion.
In a general Banach space, the identity map between primal and dual coordinates is not the appropriate unmodified interface.

notation.meaning: resolvent of the scaled operator gamma A

children.title: Minty Parametrization
children.top_down_role: Graph representations associated with Minty-type transformations.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space Minty parametrization at an arbitrary positive resolvent scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is single-valued and defined on all of \(H\). Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{gra}A
=
\left\{
\left(J_{\lambda A}z,\frac{z-J_{\lambda A}z}{\lambda}\right):z\in H
\right\}.
\]
Thus each \(z\in H\) determines exactly one graph point, and every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) is obtained from \(z=x+\lambda u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal monotone graph is parametrized by the resolvent: each ambient point yields one graph point, and every graph point arises this way.
knowledge_statements.title: Minty Parametrization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hilbert-space resolvent parametrization is mathematically standard, uses the correct representation kind, and matches the leaf, but it has no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Resolvent Range Criterion
children.top_down_role: Range structure of resolvents used to recognize maximality.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is monotone, and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is maximal monotone if and only if \(\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minty’s Hilbert-space range characterization of maximal monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following conditions are equivalent:
\[
A\text{ is maximal monotone},
\qquad
\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda A)=H.
\]
Under either condition, the inverse \(J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is an everywhere-defined single-valued mapping. If the range condition holds for one \(\lambda>0\), maximality follows and hence the range condition holds for every positive scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone Hilbert-space operator is maximal precisely when its identity shift has full range; one positive shift parameter suffices.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Range Criterion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Minty range equivalence is standard and the condition kind is appropriate, but the record lacks any source and specific theorem, section, or page locator.

children.title: Surjectivity-Based Maximality
children.top_down_role: Maximality regimes characterized through suitable surjectivity properties.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda\partial f)=H\), and therefore \(\partial f\) is maximal monotone.

notation.meaning: Proximity operator of lambda times f.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximality obtained from surjectivity of the subdifferential resolvent shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(z\in H\), the strongly convex problem
\[
\min_{x\in H}\left(f(x)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-z\|^2\right)
\]
has a unique minimizer \(x=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}z\), and its optimality condition is
\[
z\in x+\lambda\partial f(x).
\]
Consequently \(\operatorname{ran}(I+\lambda\partial f)=H\). Since \(\partial f\) is monotone, the Minty range criterion implies that \(\partial f\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every shifted subdifferential equation is solvable through a proximal minimization problem, so the subdifferential is maximal monotone by Minty’s criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Surjectivity-Based Maximality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cyclically monotone graph–potential correspondence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) have nonempty graph. A proper convex potential is a function \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) whose subdifferential contains or equals \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition and recovery of convex potentials from cyclically monotone graph data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cyclic-monotone potential correspondence assigns to a cyclically monotone operator \(A\) a function \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) satisfying \(\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}\partial f\). Conversely, every convex subdifferential \(\partial f\) is cyclically monotone. At the maximal cyclic level the correspondence is exact: \[A\text{ maximally cyclically monotone}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\text{ with }A=\partial f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cyclically monotone graph data admit a proper lower-semicontinuous convex potential whose subdifferential contains the graph. Convex subdifferentials are cyclically monotone, and maximal cyclically monotone graphs are exactly full convex subdifferential graphs.
assumptions_latex: For the containment direction, \(A\) is cyclically monotone.
For exact representation, \(A\) is maximally cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\subseteq\partial f\) for some \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), with equality when \(A\) is maximally cyclically monotone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A graph is maximally cyclically monotone exactly when it is the graph of \(\partial f\) for some \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A=\partial f\), the correspondence returns a potential differing from \(f\) by at most an additive constant when equality of subdifferentials is imposed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Cyclic monotonicity is the graph condition that encodes compatibility with a convex potential.
boundary_notes: Ordinary monotonicity alone is insufficient for this potential correspondence in general Hilbert spaces.
A containing potential need not be unique when only \(A\subseteq\partial f\) is required.

children.title: Cyclically Monotone Containment
children.top_down_role: Containment of cyclically monotone graphs in convex subdifferential graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) has a nonempty cyclically monotone graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a proper lower-semicontinuous convex \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \(\operatorname{gra}T\subseteq\operatorname{gra}\partial f\).

notation.meaning: Graph of the set-valued operator T.
Convex subdifferential graph of a potential f.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar containment theorem in a Hilbert-space formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If, for every finite cycle \((x_i,u_i)\in\operatorname{gra}T\), with \(x_{m+1}=x_1\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\langle u_i,x_{i+1}-x_i\rangle\leq0,
\]
then there exists a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfying
\[
T(x)\subseteq\partial f(x)
\quad\text{for every }x\in H.
\]
Equivalently, \(\operatorname{gra}T\subseteq\operatorname{gra}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty cyclically monotone graph is contained in the subdifferential graph of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex potential.
knowledge_statements.title: Cyclically Monotone Containment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The containment theorem and theorem content kind match the terminal container, and the cyclic-monotonicity sign convention is internally consistent, but the record provides no authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rockafellar containment potential
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be cyclically monotone with nonempty graph, and fix \((x_0,u_0)\in\operatorname{gra}A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment of a cyclically monotone graph in a convex subdifferential graph, without assuming maximality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the normalized Rockafellar potential by \[R_{A,x_0,u_0}(x)=\sup\left\{\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,u_i\rangle+\langle x-x_m,u_m\rangle\right\},\] where the supremum ranges over all integers \(m\geq0\) and all finite chains \((x_i,u_i)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) beginning at the fixed pair. Then \(R_{A,x_0,u_0}\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(R_{A,x_0,u_0}(x_0)=0\), and \[\operatorname{gra}A\subseteq\operatorname{gra}\partial R_{A,x_0,u_0}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a base graph point, take the supremum of affine chain sums generated by the cyclically monotone graph. The resulting normalized function is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex, and every original graph pair is a subgradient pair of this potential.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) and every \(y\in\mathcal H\), \(R_{A,x_0,u_0}(y)\geq R_{A,x_0,u_0}(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: The term \(m=0\) contributes the affine function \(x\mapsto\langle x-x_0,u_0\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty cyclically monotone graph possesses at least one convex subdifferential extension.
If \(A\) is already maximally cyclically monotone, the containment becomes equality.
boundary_notes: The construction depends on the selected normalization point, although additive normalization does not change a subdifferential.
Without maximal cyclic monotonicity, additional graph points may appear in \(\partial R_{A,x_0,u_0}\).

notation.meaning: normalized Rockafellar potential generated by A and the base graph point

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalized convex-potential recovery system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) have nonempty cyclically monotone graph, and fix \((x_0,u_0)\in\operatorname{gra}A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction, normalization, and uniqueness behavior of convex potentials recovered from graph data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the recovery system \[\mathfrak P(A;x_0)=\{f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\mid A\subseteq\partial f,\ f(x_0)=0\}.\] The Rockafellar chain-supremum potential belongs to \(\mathfrak P(A;x_0)\), so this system is nonempty. If \(A\) is maximally cyclically monotone, then every member satisfies \(A=\partial f\), and \(\mathfrak P(A;x_0)\) is a singleton. Without maximality, different convex extensions may produce different normalized potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recovery system consists of all proper lower-semicontinuous convex potentials normalized to zero at a chosen base point and whose subdifferentials contain the supplied graph. It is nonempty for a nonempty cyclically monotone graph. Under maximal cyclic monotonicity, containment becomes equality and normalization makes the recovered potential unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak P(A;x_0)\neq\varnothing\), and if \(A\) is maximally cyclically monotone then \(|\mathfrak P(A;x_0)|=1\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: In the maximal case, the unique normalized member is obtained from any representing potential by subtracting its value at \(x_0\).
special_cases_latex: Changing the normalization from \(f(x_0)=0\) to \(f(x_0)=c\) translates every recovered potential by \(c\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The additive-constant ambiguity is separated from genuine nonuniqueness caused by incomplete graph data.
A maximal cyclically monotone graph determines its convex potential once one scalar value is fixed.
boundary_notes: For nonmaximal graph data, normalization alone need not make the potential unique.
The base point must lie in the domain of every recovered potential; graph membership guarantees this for the displayed system.

notation.meaning: set of normalized convex potentials compatible with the graph of A

children.title: Potential Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of convex potentials from cyclically monotone graph data.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_T\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex, satisfies \(f_T(x_0)=0\), and obeys \(T(x)\subseteq\partial f_T(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Rockafellar reconstruction from a cyclically monotone graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
f_T(x)=\sup_{m\geq 0}\ \sup_{(x_i,u_i)\in\operatorname{gra}T,\ 1\leq i\leq m}
\left\{\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,u_i\rangle+\langle x-x_m,u_m\rangle\right\},
\]
where the term for \(m=0\) is \(\langle x-x_0,u_0\rangle\). Cyclic monotonicity implies \(f_T(x_0)=0\). The supremum of these affine functions is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex, and every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}T\) satisfies \(u\in\partial f_T(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the supremum of pathwise affine increments along a cyclically monotone graph reconstructs a normalized closed convex potential whose subdifferential contains that graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Potential Reconstruction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of a closed convex potential representing a nonempty subdifferential graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, \(\partial f(x)=\partial g(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f\neq\varnothing\), then there is a scalar \(c\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
f=g+c.
\]
Thus a maximal cyclically monotone operator determines its proper lower-semicontinuous convex potential only up to addition of a finite constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two proper closed convex functions with the same nonempty subdifferential operator differ by one finite additive constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive-Constant Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive-constant property is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but the record supplies no source or locator for the uniqueness theorem.

children.title: Basepoint Normalization
children.top_down_role: Normalization choices that select a representative recovered potential.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is exactly one proper lower-semicontinuous convex \(f\) satisfying \(\partial f=T\) and \(f(x_0)=a\).

notation.meaning: Prescribed basepoint in the operator domain.
Prescribed value of the potential at the basepoint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basepoint normalization removes the additive constant for maximal cyclically monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\) be maximal cyclically monotone, choose \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}T\), and prescribe \(a\in\mathbb{R}\). If \(f_T\) is any reconstructed proper lower-semicontinuous convex potential with \(\partial f_T=T\), set
\[
\widehat f_T(x)=f_T(x)-f_T(x_0)+a.
\]
Then \(\partial\widehat f_T=T\) and \(\widehat f_T(x_0)=a\). Moreover, any proper lower-semicontinuous convex \(g\) with \(\partial g=T\) and \(g(x_0)=a\) equals \(\widehat f_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prescribing one finite potential value at a point in the operator domain removes the additive-constant ambiguity and selects a unique convex potential.
knowledge_statements.title: Basepoint Normalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization condition and uniqueness conclusion fit the leaf, but both existence and uniqueness depend on uncited cyclic-monotone potential results.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential operator-interface family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) and \(\gamma>0\). Let \(f^*\) be the Fenchel conjugate and \({}^{\gamma}f(x)=\inf_y\{f(y)+\|x-y\|^2/(2\gamma)\}\) the Moreau envelope.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint Hilbert-space interface connecting conjugate inverse graphs, resolvents, proximity mappings, and Yosida regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the operator-interface family \[\mathscr I_\gamma(f)=\bigl((\partial f)^{-1},\ J_{\gamma\partial f},\ {}^{\gamma}(\partial f)\bigr).\] Its canonical identifications are \[(\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*,\qquad J_{\gamma\partial f}=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma\partial f)^{-1}=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f},\qquad {}^{\gamma}(\partial f)=\gamma^{-1}(\operatorname{Id}-J_{\gamma\partial f})=\nabla({}^{\gamma}f).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularization interface family groups three operators attached to a convex subdifferential: its inverse graph, its resolvent, and its Yosida approximation. They coincide respectively with the conjugate subdifferential, the proximal mapping, and the gradient of the Moreau envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathscr I_\gamma(f)=(\partial f^*,\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f},\nabla({}^{\gamma}f))\) under the displayed operator identifications.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(p=J_{\gamma\partial f}x\), \(\gamma^{-1}(x-p)\in\partial f(p)\).
The primal-dual graph symmetry is \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\iff(u,x)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f^*\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\gamma=1\), \(J_{\partial f}=\operatorname{Prox}_f\).
For \(f=\iota_C\), the resolvent is the metric projection \(P_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The generally set-valued subdifferential produces an everywhere-defined single-valued proximity operator.
The Yosida approximation supplies a single-valued gradient representation of the regularized operator.
boundary_notes: These identities use Hilbert-space quadratic regularization and the Riesz identification.
The family does not assert differentiability of \(f\) itself.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the Fenchel--Young inequality is exact precisely on the subdifferential graph:
\[
u\in\partial f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle u,x\rangle
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in\partial f^*(u).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{gra}\partial f^*=\{(u,x):(x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\},
\qquad
\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugation exchanges the coordinates of a convex subdifferential graph: a vector subgradient of the primal point makes that point a subgradient of the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Inverse-Graph Symmetry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate subdifferential inverse symmetry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), and define \(f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal H}(\langle x,u\rangle-f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual symmetry of convex subdifferential graphs in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conjugate inverse-graph symmetry is \[u\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle x,u\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(u).\] Equivalently, \[(\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*,\qquad \operatorname{gra}\partial f^*=\{(u,x)\mid(x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector \(u\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) exactly when the Fenchel–Young inequality is an equality, and this is equivalent to \(x\) being a subgradient of the conjugate at \(u\). Thus conjugation swaps the two coordinates of the subdifferential graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in\partial f(x)\iff x\in\partial f^*(u)\), hence \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(u\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle x,u\rangle\).
The coordinate-swap map \((x,u)\mapsto(u,x)\) carries \(\operatorname{gra}\partial f\) onto \(\operatorname{gra}\partial f^*\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f(x)=\|x\|^2/2\), then \(f^*=f\) and \(\partial f=\operatorname{Id}\), so the graph is invariant under coordinate exchange.
immediate_consequences_latex: Primal subgradient inclusions and dual subgradient inclusions encode the same graph point.
The domains and ranges satisfy \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*=\operatorname{ran}\partial f\).
boundary_notes: For a merely proper nonclosed function, the implication to \(x\in\partial f^*(u)\) need not yield the full reverse equivalence without the closed-convex hypothesis.
The equality is between set-valued operators, not pointwise equality of \(f\) and \(f^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x,p\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(z)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert z-x\rVert^2\right\}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x-p\in\lambda\partial f(p).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}=J_{\lambda\partial f}=\left(I+\lambda\partial f\right)^{-1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal mapping of a proper closed convex function is the resolvent of its scaled subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximity operator as a subdifferential resolvent
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), and \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator bridge between quadratic proximal minimization and the resolvent of a convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proximal–resolvent interface is the everywhere-defined mapping \[\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}(x)=\underset{y\in\mathcal H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|x-y\|^2\right\}=J_{\gamma\partial f}(x)=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma\partial f)^{-1}(x).\] Its pointwise inclusion form is \[p=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-p\in\gamma\partial f(p).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal mapping of \(\gamma f\) is the resolvent of the scaled subdifferential. Its value is the unique minimizer of the quadratically regularized objective, and a point \(p\) is this minimizer exactly when \(x-p\) belongs to \(\gamma\partial f(p)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}(x)\iff0\in\partial f(p)+\gamma^{-1}(p-x)\).
\(p=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}(x)\iff(p,\gamma^{-1}(x-p))\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\gamma=1\), \(\operatorname{Prox}_f=(\operatorname{Id}+\partial f)^{-1}\).
For \(f=\iota_C\) with \(C\) nonempty, closed, and convex, \(\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}=P_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The proximity operator is single-valued and has domain \(\mathcal H\).
Its range is contained in \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\).
boundary_notes: The quadratic term and the displayed resolvent identity use Hilbert-space geometry.
The proximal mapping is not generally the ordinary gradient of \(f\).

notation.meaning: proximity operator of the scaled function gamma f

children.top_down_role: Regularized and single-valued approximations of subdifferential operators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla e_\lambda f=(\partial f)_\lambda=\lambda^{-1}(I-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f})\), and this operator is single-valued and \(\lambda^{-1}\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Moreau envelope and Yosida approximation of a convex subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: 6.6 Moreau Decomposition p. 160
source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
e_\lambda f(x)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(z)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert z-x\rVert^2\right\},
\qquad
(\partial f)_\lambda=\frac{1}{\lambda}\left(I-(I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}\right).
\]
Then \(e_\lambda f\) is finite-valued, convex, and continuously differentiable, and
\[
\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=(\partial f)_\lambda(x)=\frac{x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)}{\lambda}.
\]
The resulting operator is single-valued, monotone, and \(\lambda^{-1}\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the gradient of the Moreau envelope is the Yosida approximation of the subdifferential and the scaled residual of the proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.title: Moreau–Yosida Interface

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau Envelope and Yosida Approximation of a Convex Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(M:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be symmetric positive definite. Write \(W=M^{-1}\) and use the Euclidean dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex Moreau regularization with a positive-definite quadratic metric; both the regularized function and the induced single-valued subgradient approximation are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[f_M(x):=\min_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{f(y)+\frac12\langle M(y-x),y-x\rangle\right\},\qquad p_M(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{f(y)+\frac12\langle M(y-x),y-x\rangle\right\}.\] The minimizer is unique. The Moreau–Yosida interface associated with \((f,M)\) is the pair \((p_M,s_M)\), where \[s_M(x):=M(x-p_M(x)).\] It satisfies \[s_M(x)\in\partial f(p_M(x)),\qquad p_M(x)=x-Ws_M(x),\qquad \nabla f_M(x)=s_M(x).\] Equivalently, \(p_M=(I+W\partial f)^{-1}\) and \(s_M=(\partial f)_{W}\) is the corresponding single-valued Yosida approximation. In the scalar metric \(M=\lambda^{-1}I\), these become \[e_\lambda f(x)=\min_y\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-y\|^2\right\},\quad \operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=p_M(x),\quad \nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function and a positive-definite quadratic metric, the Moreau envelope is the minimum of the function plus the quadratic displacement cost. Its unique minimizer is the proximal point. Multiplying the residual from the proximal point to the center by the metric gives a distinguished subgradient at the proximal point, and this vector is exactly the gradient of the envelope. Thus the interface replaces the set-valued subdifferential by a globally defined single-valued approximation while retaining an exact graph point of the original subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[0\in\partial f(p_M(x))+M(p_M(x)-x).\]
special_cases_latex: For \(M=\lambda^{-1}I\), \(p_M=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\) and \(s_M=\lambda^{-1}(I-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f})\).
For \(f=\delta_C\) with \(C\) nonempty, closed, and convex, \(p_I=P_C\) and \(f_I=\tfrac12 d_C^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(f_M\) is finite, convex, and continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(\nabla f_M\) is Lipschitz with constant at most \(\lambda_{\max}(M)\) in the Euclidean norm.
boundary_notes: Positive semidefinite but singular metrics do not provide the stated global uniqueness without additional hypotheses.
This definition does not assert second differentiability of \(f_M\).

notation.meaning: Yosida subgradient selected by the proximal residual

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Family of Structure-Certified Subgradient Representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\) denote the proper closed convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\). For \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\) and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), a representation may use constituent functions, affine maps, active sets, exposed faces, or optimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal family of subdifferential descriptions assembled from recognized convex representations; it excludes iterative optimization procedures and their complexity analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structural subgradient construction for \((f,x)\) is a finite specification \(\mathcal R=(\mathcal D,\mathcal O,\mathcal Q,S_{\mathcal R}(x))\) such that: \(\mathcal D\) decomposes \(f\) into convex constituents; \(\mathcal O\) records the convexity-preserving operations joining them; \(\mathcal Q\) records every qualification used by an exact calculus rule; and \(S_{\mathcal R}(x)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is obtained from constituent subdifferentials by the corresponding set operations. It is exact when \[S_{\mathcal R}(x)=\partial f(x),\] an inner construction when \[S_{\mathcal R}(x)\subseteq\partial f(x),\] and an outer construction when \[\partial f(x)\subseteq S_{\mathcal R}(x).\] The structural construction family is \[\mathfrak S:=\{(f,x,\mathcal R):f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n),\ x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \mathcal R\text{ satisfies one of the three certified relations above}\}.\] Permitted structural operations include positive sums, affine precomposition, increasing convex composition, finite maxima, suitably regular compact suprema, exact marginalization, and exact infimal convolution. Each occurrence of an equality rule must carry its own qualification; an unconditional inclusion is not promoted to equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural subgradient construction is a finite certificate that decomposes a convex function, records the operations used to build it, states all qualifications needed by the relevant calculus rules, and produces a set of candidate subgradients from the constituents. The certificate explicitly labels the resulting set as exact, inner, or outer according to its relation with the true subdifferential. The family contains these certified representations, not algorithms for finding an optimizer or convergence claims about such algorithms.
assumptions_latex: Every constituent subdifferential and every set operation in \(S_{\mathcal R}(x)\) is well-defined.
Every exact rule in \(\mathcal O\) satisfies the qualification recorded in \(\mathcal Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(f,x,\mathcal R)\in\mathfrak S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S_{\mathcal R}(x)\text{ has a certified exact, inner, or outer relation to }\partial f(x).\]
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\sum_i t_i f_i\) with finite convex constituents and \(t_i>0\), the exact construction is \(S_{\mathcal R}(x)=\sum_i t_i\partial f_i(x)\).
For \(f=\max_i f_i\), the active-index construction is \(S_{\mathcal R}(x)=\operatorname{co}\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A representation can expose a single member of \(\partial f(x)\) without enumerating the full set.
The qualification record distinguishes exact calculus from fallback inclusions.
boundary_notes: The family is a mathematical taxonomy of representation certificates, not a numerical oracle model by itself.
Nonconvex generalized gradients and stochastic estimators are outside this definition.

notation.meaning: family of certified structural subgradient constructions
set produced by structural representation R at x

children.title: Calculus-Based Construction
children.top_down_role: Composable subgradient descriptions built from recognized convex operations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recursive Convex Subdifferential Calculus Construction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an expression \(E\) represent a finite-valued convex function \(f_E:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\). Leaves are convex functions with known subdifferentials, and internal nodes are recognized convex operations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finite-valued convex calculus, where the standard sum, affine-chain, monotone-composition, and maximum rules are exact without extended-domain qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the calculus construction \(\mathcal C(E,x)\) recursively. At a leaf \(E=h\), set \(\mathcal C(E,x)=\partial h(x)\). For positive sums, affine precomposition, and finite maxima, set respectively \[\mathcal C\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m t_iE_i,x\right)=\sum_{i=1}^m t_i\mathcal C(E_i,x),\qquad t_i>0,\] \[\mathcal C(g\circ A,x)=A_0^*\mathcal C(g,Ax),\qquad A(x)=A_0x+b,\] and \[\mathcal C\!\left(\max_{1\le i\le m}E_i,x\right)=\operatorname{co}\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\mathcal C(E_i,x),\quad I(x)=\{i:f_{E_i}(x)=f_E(x)\}.\] If \(F=(f_{E_1},\ldots,f_{E_m})\) and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is convex and componentwise nondecreasing, define \[\mathcal C(g\circ F,x)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\rho_i s_i:\rho\in\partial g(F(x)),\ s_i\in\mathcal C(E_i,x)\right\}.\] An expression is calculus-constructible at \(x\) when this recursion terminates at recognized leaves. For every such expression in this regime, \[\mathcal C(E,x)=\partial f_E(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A calculus-based construction recursively computes the subdifferential of a convex expression from the subdifferentials of its leaves. Positive sums become Minkowski sums, affine precomposition pulls subgradients back by the adjoint linear map, componentwise increasing convex composition forms weighted sums, and a finite maximum takes the convex hull of the subdifferentials of active pieces. In the stated finite-valued regime, the recursively produced set equals the subdifferential of the represented function.
assumptions_latex: Every leaf is a finite-valued convex function on its stated Euclidean space.
Every scalar coefficient in a positive sum satisfies \(t_i>0\).
The outer function in a vector composition is convex and componentwise nondecreasing.
All affine maps and adjoints have compatible dimensions.
special_cases_latex: If all active pieces are differentiable, \(\partial\max_i f_i(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\).
If \(g\) is differentiable, its unique weight vector \(\nabla g(F(x))\) gives a weighted Minkowski sum.
immediate_consequences_latex: The construction preserves an explicit decomposition of each resulting subgradient into constituent subgradients.
Nonsmoothness created by a maximum is represented by convex multipliers on active pieces.
boundary_notes: Extended-valued functions require separate domain qualifications and are not covered by the unconditional equalities stated here.
Negative linear combinations generally destroy convexity and do not satisfy the positive-sum rule.

notation.meaning: subgradient set recursively constructed from expression E at x
active index set of a finite maximum

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\). Represent \(F\) by a finite expression tree over \(\mathbb{R}^n\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Expression Tree and Induced Subdifferential Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a rooted finite expression tree whose leaves \(E_j\) represent convex functions and whose internal nodes represent operations with stated subdifferential rules.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A syntax-directed mathematical decomposition of a convex expression; the definition separates the expression tree from the qualifications that validate exact propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An expression-structure decomposition of a convex function \(f\) at \(x\) is a triple \((E,\operatorname{val},\operatorname{sub})\) satisfying: the root value is \(\operatorname{val}(E)=f\); every leaf \(L\) has a specified convex value function \(f_L\) and set \(\operatorname{sub}(L,x)=\partial f_L(x)\); and every internal node \(N=\omega(N_1,\ldots,N_k)\) has \[\operatorname{val}(N)=\omega(\operatorname{val}(N_1),\ldots,\operatorname{val}(N_k))\] together with a rule map \(R_\omega\) such that \[\operatorname{sub}(N,x)=R_\omega\bigl(x;\operatorname{sub}(N_1,\xi_1(x)),\ldots,\operatorname{sub}(N_k,\xi_k(x))\bigr).\] The decomposition is exact at \(x\) if each internal rule is exact under its recorded qualification and \[\operatorname{sub}(E,x)=\partial f(x).\] It is inclusion-valid if every rule is directionally valid and the root relation is explicitly recorded as either \(\operatorname{sub}(E,x)\subseteq\partial f(x)\) or \(\partial f(x)\subseteq\operatorname{sub}(E,x)\). Thus identical value functions may have different decompositions, but a decomposition is identified by its tree, evaluation points, rule maps, and qualifications—not merely by the root formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression-structure decomposition is a finite rooted tree for a convex formula. Leaves carry known subdifferentials. Each internal node carries both the operation producing its value and the rule that propagates subgradient sets from its children, including any shifted evaluation points. The decomposition is exact only when every rule's qualification is recorded and valid; otherwise it must retain the direction of the supported inclusion. Two algebraically equal formulas can therefore define different decompositions and different computational representations.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and every node has a well-defined convex value function on its ambient space.
Every rule map \(R_\omega\) has dimensionally compatible arguments.
Qualifications are evaluated at the node where the associated rule is applied.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The tree may be represented as a directed acyclic graph when identical subexpressions are shared, provided node values and rule maps remain unchanged.
special_cases_latex: A maximum node stores its active child set \(I(x)\) and applies convex hull to their subdifferentials.
An affine-composition node stores the adjoint \(A_0^*\) and evaluates its child at \(Ax\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The decomposition supplies provenance for every constituent of a constructed subgradient.
Local rule qualifications can be checked independently at separate internal nodes.
boundary_notes: This object does not prescribe an evaluation order or numerical data structure.
Algebraic simplification is not assumed to preserve a chosen decomposition certificate.

notation.meaning: convex function represented by node N
subgradient set propagated at node N
set-valued calculus rule attached to operation omega

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact, Inclusion, and Closure Regimes for Convex Subdifferential Rules
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,f_2\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\), let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f_1\cap\operatorname{dom}f_2\), and let \(R(x)\) denote the set produced by a proposed subdifferential calculus rule.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-valued convex calculus, with the sum rule as the canonical classifier for qualification-sensitive exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A qualification-exactness regime for a rule \(R\) is the label determined by its strongest supported relation to the target subdifferential: \[\operatorname{Reg}(R,x)=\begin{cases}\mathrm{EXACT},&R(x)=\partial f(x),\\ \mathrm{INNER},&R(x)\subseteq\partial f(x)\text{ and equality is not certified},\\ \mathrm{OUTER},&\partial f(x)\subseteq R(x)\text{ and equality is not certified},\\ \mathrm{CLOSURE},&\partial f(x)=\operatorname{cl}R(x)\text{ while }R(x)\text{ need not be closed}.\end{cases}\] For the sum \(f=f_1+f_2\), one always has \[\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x)\subseteq\partial(f_1+f_2)(x).\] The rule is in the exact regime whenever a standard qualification such as \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_1)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2)\ne\varnothing\] holds; then \[\partial(f_1+f_2)(x)=\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x).\] At the approximate level, exactness means \[\partial_\varepsilon(f_1+f_2)(x)=\bigcup_{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2\le\varepsilon}\bigl(\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f_1(x)+\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f_2(x)\bigr),\] under the corresponding exact-conjugate condition. Without qualification, only the displayed inclusion is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The taxonomy labels a calculus formula by the strongest relation actually certified between its constructed set and the true subdifferential: equality, inner inclusion, outer inclusion, or equality only after closure. For extended-valued convex sums, adding constituent subgradients always gives valid subgradients of the sum, but the reverse inclusion requires a qualification. Intersecting the relative interiors of the effective domains is a standard sufficient qualification for exactness. The same distinction persists for approximate subdifferentials through the allocation of the error budget among constituents.
assumptions_latex: For the exact label, the stated relative-interior or equivalent exact-conjugate qualification holds.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For two convex sets, \(\operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2\ne\varnothing\) is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(C_1-C_2)\).
special_cases_latex: If one summand is finite and continuous everywhere, the relative-interior qualification holds whenever the other summand is proper.
For finite-valued convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\), the positive-sum rule is exact everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: A failed qualification does not invalidate the inner inclusion.
Closure must be retained explicitly when a generated Minkowski sum or image is not known to be closed.
boundary_notes: Failure of a sufficient qualification does not itself prove that equality fails.
The taxonomy records mathematical validity, not the numerical cost of evaluating either side.

notation.meaning: exactness label assigned to rule R at x

children.title: Qualification Conditions
children.top_down_role: Constraint qualifications governing the availability of exact subdifferential calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions for \(1\leq i\leq m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\), the exact finite-sum rule \(\partial(\sum_i f_i)(x)=\sum_i\partial f_i(x)\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior qualification for the finite-dimensional convex subdifferential sum rule.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Calculus Rules p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the condition
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\neq\varnothing
\]
is a qualification ensuring exact subdifferential addition. Under this condition, every \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\) satisfies
\[
\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common point in the relative interiors of all effective domains qualifies the finite-dimensional sum rule and permits exact addition of subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Conditions

children.title: Exact Calculus Regime
children.top_down_role: Settings where calculus constructions yield exact subdifferential descriptions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every subgradient of \(\sum_i f_i\) at \(x\) decomposes exactly as \(u=\sum_i u_i\) with \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau–Rockafellar exact sum rule in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Calculus Rules p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\). If
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\neq\varnothing,
\]
then, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\),
\[
\partial F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x).
\]
Equivalently, \(u\in\partial F(x)\) if and only if there exist \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\) such that \(u=\sum_{i=1}^m u_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the relative-interior qualification, every subgradient of a finite convex sum is exactly a sum of component subgradients, and every such sum is valid.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Calculus Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Calculus Rules p. 27

children.title: Inclusion-Only Fallbacks
children.top_down_role: Cases where available calculus supports only one-sided set inclusion.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\subseteq\partial(f+g)(x)\); without an exactness qualification, the reverse inclusion is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the two subdifferential sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Always-valid one-sided finite-dimensional sum rule when exactness qualifications are unavailable.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Calculus Rules p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For proper convex functions \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\),
\[
\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\subseteq\partial(f+g)(x).
\]
Without a suitable qualification condition, the reverse inclusion can fail; the displayed inclusion is the generally valid fallback.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component subgradients always combine to give a subgradient of a convex sum, but a sum subgradient need not decompose into component subgradients without qualification.
knowledge_statements.title: Inclusion-Only Fallbacks

children.title: Closure-Dependent Rules
children.top_down_role: Calculus descriptions whose validity requires a closure operation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f+g)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f^*\mathbin{\square}g^*)\); removing the closure requires additional exactness conditions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conjugate sum calculus when infimal-convolution exactness is unavailable.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 A Glimpse of Biconjugate Calculus p. 71
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms II: Advanced Theory and Bundle Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the infimal convolution by
\[
(f^*\mathbin{\square}g^*)(u)=\inf_{v\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{f^*(v)+g^*(u-v)\}.
\]
When this function is proper, biconjugate calculus gives
\[
(f+g)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f^*\mathbin{\square}g^*).
\]
Thus an unqualified dual decomposition may determine the conjugate only after lower-semicontinuous closure. Equality without closure, together with attainment of the displayed infimum at the relevant \(u\), is an additional exactness property rather than an unconditional rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without qualification, conjugating a convex sum may require closing the infimal convolution; an exact dual subgradient decomposition additionally depends on equality without closure and attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Dependent Rules

children.top_down_role: Subgradient representations obtained from active pieces, maximizing faces, and optimizer sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extraction of Active Generators from a Supremum Representation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\) be compact, let \(f_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex for \(j\in J\), assume \(j\mapsto f_j(x)\) is upper semicontinuous for every \(x\), and define \(f(x)=\sup_{j\in J}f_j(x)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex supremum models with compact, upper-semicontinuous index dependence; active indices may encode pieces, exposed points, or optimizer solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The active structure at \(x\) is the nonempty compact set \[J(x):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{j\in J}f_j(x)=\{j\in J:f_j(x)=f(x)\}.\] Its extracted subgradient generator set and active hull are \[G(x):=\bigcup_{j\in J(x)}\partial f_j(x),\qquad H(x):=\operatorname{co}G(x).\] Under the stated compactness and upper-semicontinuity conditions, active-structure extraction is the exact representation \[\partial f(x)=H(x)=\operatorname{co}\bigcup_{j\in J(x)}\partial f_j(x).\] If every active constituent is differentiable at \(x\), this reduces to \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_j(x):j\in J(x)\}.\] A selected active index \(j_x\in J(x)\) supplies the certified subgradient inclusion \[\partial f_{j_x}(x)\subseteq\partial f(x),\] so any \(g\in\partial f_{j_x}(x)\) is valid even when the full active hull is not enumerated. The term active structure refers to \(J(x)\), together with the constituent subgradient sets attached to its members.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function represented as a compact supremum, the active structure at a point is the set of indices attaining the supremum. Extracting all subdifferentials attached to those indices and taking their convex hull gives the complete subdifferential under the stated regularity assumptions. If the pieces are differentiable, only their active gradients are needed. Selecting just one active piece still yields a valid subgradient, although it need not recover the whole subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_j\) is finite-valued and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
For every \(x\), the map \(j\mapsto f_j(x)\) is upper semicontinuous.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(f_j(\cdot)=g(\cdot,j)\), then \(J(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{j\in J}g(x,j)\).
special_cases_latex: For finite \(J\), compactness and upper semicontinuity are automatic.
For a support function \(f=\sigma_C\), the active set is the exposed face \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A single optimizer of the inner maximization can expose one valid subgradient.
Multiple active pieces account precisely for convex combinations in the subdifferential.
boundary_notes: If the index set is not compact or the index dependence is not upper semicontinuous, active indices may be absent and the equality can fail.
Approximate maximizers require an approximate-subdifferential formulation not included here.

notation.meaning: active or maximizing index set at x

children.title: Active-Index Models
children.top_down_role: Active-component representations for maxima and piecewise functions.

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex and continuous near \(x\) for \(1\leq i\leq m\).

notation.meaning: Set of components attaining the maximum at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maximum rule using the subdifferentials of active convex components.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Calculus Rules p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the active index set
\[
I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f_i(x)=F(x)\}.
\]
For the finite maximum \(F=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i\), continuity of the convex components near \(x\) yields
\[
\partial F(x)=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).
\]
Equivalently, every \(u\in\partial F(x)\) has a representation \(u=\sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i u_i\), where \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\), \(\alpha_i\geq0\), and \(\sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite convex maximum is the convex hull of subgradients from exactly those components attaining the maximum at the evaluation point.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Index Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Active-Index Subdifferential Model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and set \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maxima and finite piecewise-convex models; all constituent functions are finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The active-index model of \(f\) at \(x\) is the pair \((I(x),\mathcal G(x))\) defined by \[I(x):=\{i\in\{1,,m\}:f_i(x)=f(x)\},\qquad \mathcal G(x):=\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x).\] Its represented subdifferential is \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\mathcal G(x)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i g_i:\alpha_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i=1,\ g_i\in\partial f_i(x)\right\}.\] If the pieces are differentiable, the model becomes \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}.\] For a piecewise-affine function \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{a_i+\langle s_i,x\rangle\},\] the model is finitely generated: \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{s_i:i\in I(x)\}.\] Thus inactive pieces contribute no generator at \(x\), while every convex combination of active constituent subgradients is represented.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite maximum of convex functions, the active index set consists of the pieces attaining the maximum at the point. The subdifferential is exactly the convex hull of the subdifferentials of those active pieces. When the pieces are smooth, their active gradients are the generators; when they are affine, the corresponding slope vectors generate a polytope. Inactive pieces make no contribution at that point.
assumptions_latex: The evaluation point \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is arbitrary.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[g\in\partial f(x)\iff \exists\alpha\in\Delta_{I(x)},\ g_i\in\partial f_i(x):g=\sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i g_i.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(I(x)=\{i_0\}\) and \(f_{i_0}\) is differentiable, then \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f_{i_0}(x)\}\).
For \(f(x)=\max_i(a_i+\langle s_i,x\rangle)\), active slopes \(s_i\) are the only generators.
immediate_consequences_latex: Nondifferentiability occurs whenever the active generator hull is not a singleton.
Any active constituent subgradient is itself a subgradient of the maximum.
boundary_notes: This finite formula does not by itself cover a nonattained infinite supremum.
A piecewise representation that is not globally a maximum of convex pieces may require a different generalized derivative.

notation.meaning: simplex of convex weights supported on active indices

children.title: Exposed-Face Models
children.top_down_role: Face-based representations for support functions, gauges, and norms.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset E\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.

notation.meaning: Face of C exposed by x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exposed-face formulas for support functions and closed gauges.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Support Functions p. 135
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in E\), the support function satisfies \[\partial\sigma_C(x)=F_C(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in C}\langle x,u\rangle.\] If additionally \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then the gauge is the support function of the polar, \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\), and for every \(x\in E\), \[\partial\gamma_C(x)=\{y\in C^\circ:\langle y,x\rangle=\gamma_C(x)\}.\] Thus its subgradients form the face of \(C^\circ\) exposed by \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support function's subdifferential is its maximizing exposed face. A gauge has the analogous representation through the exposed face of its polar set.
knowledge_statements.title: Exposed-Face Models
