knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hierarchy of ambient regimes for subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, where \(X\) is respectively \(\mathbb R^n\), a real Hilbert space \(H\), or a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A regime index specifying the ambient pairing and topologies before a subdifferential statement is interpreted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dimension-topology regime descriptor is
\[\mathfrak R(X)=(\mathcal P,\tau_p,\tau_d,\mathcal K),\]
where \(\mathcal P\) is the primal-dual pairing used in the subgradient inequality, \(\tau_p\) and \(\tau_d\) are the declared primal and dual topologies, and \(\mathcal K\) records the compactness principle available to the statement. In the finite-dimensional regime, \(X=X^*=\mathbb R^n\), \(\mathcal P=\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), compatible vector topologies coincide, and bounded closed sets are compact. In the Hilbert regime, the Riesz map identifies \(H^*\) with \(H\), but norm and weak topologies differ in infinite dimension; bounded closed convex sets are weakly compact. In the Banach regime, subgradients lie in \(X^*\), pairing is \(\langle x^*,x\rangle\), and norm, weak, and weak-star closure or convergence must be distinguished. A subdifferential claim is regime-complete only after these components are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hierarchy records four pieces of ambient information: the primal-dual pairing, the primal topology, the dual topology, and the compactness mechanism. Euclidean spaces identify primal and dual and have ordinary compactness of bounded closed sets. Hilbert spaces retain a vector identification through the Riesz map but distinguish weak and norm behavior. General Banach spaces use a separate dual and require explicit weak-star choices. Statements should not be transferred between these regimes without checking those components.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is one of the three stated classes of real spaces.
All duals are continuous duals for the declared norm topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak R(X)\) fixes the pairing and topology needed to interpret \(\partial f\), closure, compactness, and convergence.
special_cases_latex: Every finite-dimensional Hilbert space belongs simultaneously to the Euclidean and Hilbert descriptions, with weak and norm topologies coinciding.
immediate_consequences_latex: A sequential closure statement in a dual space is incomplete unless the dual topology is specified.
boundary_notes: Asplundness is an additional Banach-space property, not a consequence of being Banach.
The descriptor is a local organizational definition rather than a standard named hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-dimensional convex-subdifferential regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with the Euclidean pairing \(\langle g,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex analysis, including lower-dimensional effective domains handled by relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite-dimensional subdifferential regime consists of statements interpreted with
\[\partial f(x)=\{g\in\mathbb R^n:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle g,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in\mathbb R^n\},\]
Euclidean closure, and relative interior taken in \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Its characteristic existence guarantee is
\[x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Longrightarrow\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing.\]
If \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), then \(\partial f(x)\) is nonempty, closed, and bounded, hence compact. For a finite convex function on all of \(\mathbb R^n\), these properties hold at every point, and the directional derivative satisfies
\[f'(x;d)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle.\]
The regime also uses common-relative-interior qualifications for exact finite sums and normal-cone intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, subgradients are vectors in the same Euclidean space. Relative interior handles domains contained in lower-dimensional affine sets and guarantees subgradient existence there. At ordinary interior points the subdifferential is bounded as well as closed, so finite-dimensional compactness applies. A finite convex function on the whole space therefore has a nonempty compact subdifferential everywhere, and its directional derivative is the support function of that set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative-interior points have nonempty subdifferentials; interior points have nonempty compact subdifferentials.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite convex \(f\), \(f'(x;\cdot)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}\) at every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
special_cases_latex: For polyhedral convex \(f\), every point of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is subdifferentiable and \(\partial f(x)\) is polyhedral.
immediate_consequences_latex: Euclidean bounded sequences admit convergent subsequences, a fact not available in the strong topology of infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
boundary_notes: At a relative-boundary point, subgradient existence is not guaranteed.
Ambient subdifferentials can be unbounded when the effective domain has a proper affine hull.

children.title: Hilbert-Space Regime
children.top_down_role: Inner-product geometry, mixed graph topologies, and resolvent interfaces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{Id}+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\), an everywhere-defined single-valued firmly nonexpansive map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space resolvent representation of the convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), the strongly convex problem \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{y\in H}\;f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\] has a unique solution \(p\). Its optimality condition is \(x-p\in\lambda\partial f(p)\), and therefore \[p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}(x).\] The resolvent is defined on all of \(H\), is single-valued, and is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In Hilbert space, the resolvent of a convex subdifferential is the everywhere-defined, firmly nonexpansive proximity operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert-Space Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically standard and well matched to the Hilbert-space regime, but the record supplies no citation for the resolvent-proximity identity, global single-valuedness, or firm nonexpansiveness. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hilbert-space subdifferential and resolvent regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces; dual vectors are identified with primal vectors using Riesz representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Hilbert-space convex subdifferential is the set-valued operator
\[\partial f:H\rightrightarrows H,\qquad \partial f(x)=\{u\in H:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\ \forall y\in H\}.\]
The Hilbert regime uses the Riesz identification \(H^*\simeq H\), so \(\partial f\) can be added to the identity operator. For \(\gamma>0\), its resolvent is
\[J_{\gamma\partial f}=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma\partial f)^{-1}=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f},\]
and
\[p=J_{\gamma\partial f}(x)\iff \gamma^{-1}(x-p)\in\partial f(p).\]
Topology remains explicit: norm convergence and weak convergence differ in infinite dimension, although bounded closed convex subsets are weakly compact. Thus weak-strong graph limits, weak compactness, and strong resolvent evaluations are not interchangeable without a stated topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a Hilbert space, Riesz representation identifies continuous linear functionals with vectors, so subgradients belong to the same space as primal points. This permits the identity-plus-subdifferential resolvent. For a closed proper convex function the resolvent is its proximity operator, and its defining inclusion links a proximal point to a subgradient. Infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces still distinguish norm and weak convergence, even though bounded closed convex sets are weakly compact.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(J_{\gamma\partial f}=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}\) are the canonical Hilbert-space interfaces.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(u\in\partial f(x)\iff f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\ \forall y\in H\).
\(p=J_{\gamma\partial f}(x)\iff x-p\in\gamma\partial f(p)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\iota_C\) with \(C\) nonempty closed and convex, \(J_{\gamma\partial f}=P_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The Riesz identification is what makes \(\operatorname{Id}+\partial f\) an operator sum on one space.
boundary_notes: Weak and strong convergence coincide only in finite dimensions.
The Riesz identification is unavailable in a general Banach space without an additional duality map.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Banach dual-pair and Asplund regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Banach space with continuous dual \(X^*\), canonical pairing \(\langle x^*,x\rangle\), and weak-star topology \(\sigma(X^*,X)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General Banach spaces and the Asplund subclass; primal and dual spaces are not identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the Banach-space convex subdifferential is
\[\partial f(x)=\{x^*\in X^*:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle x^*,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in X\}.\]
A Banach topological regime is specified by declaring norm, weak, or weak-star topology for every closure and limit involving \(X\) or \(X^*\). The regime is Asplund when every continuous convex real-valued function on every nonempty open convex subset of \(X\) is Fréchet differentiable on a dense \(G_\delta\) subset. In this subclass, dense differentiability and approximation by Fréchet subgradients support limiting constructions unavailable in arbitrary Banach spaces. The descriptor therefore consists of \((X,X^*,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle,\tau_X,\tau_{X^*},a_X)\), where \(a_X\) records whether \(X\) is Asplund.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a Banach space, convex subgradients are continuous linear functionals in the separate dual space. Every closure and convergence assertion must state whether it uses norm, weak, or weak-star topology. An Asplund space is distinguished by generic Fréchet differentiability of continuous convex functions on open convex sets. This property enables stronger approximation-based nonsmooth analysis than is available in a completely general Banach space.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space and \(X^*\) is its continuous dual.
The topology of each closure or limit is explicitly declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Banach-Asplund regime is determined by the dual pairing, chosen topologies, and the Asplund differentiability property.
special_cases_latex: Every Hilbert space is Asplund, but its Riesz identification provides additional structure not included in the general Banach descriptor.
immediate_consequences_latex: An unqualified symbol \(\operatorname{cl}\) is ambiguous for subsets of \(X^*\) when norm and weak-star closures can differ.
boundary_notes: The Asplund characterization and approximation consequences require an authoritative Banach-space source.
A general Banach space need not have the stated generic Fréchet differentiability property.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\) is Asplund exactly when every continuous convex function on an open convex subset is Fréchet differentiable on a dense \(G_\delta\) subset.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Banach space \(X\) is Asplund if every separable closed subspace \(Y\subseteq X\) has separable dual \(Y^*\). Equivalently, for every nonempty open convex set \(U\subseteq X\) and every continuous convex function \(f:U\to\mathbb R\), the set of points at which \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable contains a dense \(G_\delta\) subset of \(U\). This generic differentiability property distinguishes the Asplund regime in nonsmooth subdifferential calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asplund spaces are precisely Banach spaces where continuous convex functions are generically Fréchet differentiable on open convex domains.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)\) is weak-star closed and convex; each bounded slice \(\partial f(x)\cap rB_{X^*}\) is weak-star compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the set \[\partial f(x)=\bigcap_{y\in X}\{x^*\in X^*: \langle x^*,y-x\rangle\leq f(y)-f(x)\}\] is convex and closed for the weak-star topology \(\sigma(X^*,X)\). For every \(r>0\), its bounded slice \(\partial f(x)\cap rB_{X^*}\) is weak-star compact. The entire subdifferential is weak-star compact only when it is norm bounded; weak-star closedness alone does not imply compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subdifferentials are weak-star closed; bounded slices are weak-star compact, but an unbounded subdifferential need not be compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(f^*(x^*)=\sup_{y\in X}(\langle x^*,y\rangle-f(y))\), Fenchel–Young inequality gives \(f(x)+f^*(x^*)\geq\langle x^*,x\rangle\). Equality holds precisely when \[x^*\in\partial f(x).\] Because \(f=f^{**}\) under the canonical embedding of \(X\) into \(X^{**}\), the same equality is equivalent to \(x\in\partial f^*(x^*)\). Thus the duality pairing, rather than an inner product identification, governs Banach-space subgradient inversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel–Young equality is equivalent to reciprocal primal and dual subgradient relations under the Banach-space dual pairing.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(x\) if and only if \(\partial f(x)\) is a singleton; then its unique member is the Gâteaux derivative. If \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\), necessarily \(\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}\) and \[f(x+h)=f(x)+\langle Df(x),h\rangle+o(\lVert h\rVert).\] In an infinite-dimensional Banach space, singleton-valuedness alone does not ensure this norm-uniform remainder, so it does not generally imply Fréchet differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singleton convex subdifferential characterizes Gâteaux differentiability, but in infinite dimensions it need not imply Fréchet differentiability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiability Characterized by a Unique Convex Subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper convex functions at interior points of their effective domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\). Conversely, if \(f\) has a unique subgradient at \(x\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), and its unique subgradient is \(\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function at an interior-domain point, differentiability makes the subdifferential the singleton containing the gradient, while uniqueness of the subgradient conversely implies differentiability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is differentiable at }x\iff \partial f(x)\text{ is a singleton},\quad\text{and then }\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiability transfer at an attained infimal convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers Gâteaux or Fréchet differentiability from one summand to the infimal convolution at an attained decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) and \(x,y\in\mathcal H\). Suppose \(f\square g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \((f\square g)(x)=f(y)+g(x-y)\), and \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(y\). Then \(x\in\operatorname{cont}(f\square g)\), \(f\square g\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(x\), and \(\nabla(f\square g)(x)=\nabla f(y)\). If, in addition, \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(y\), then \(f\square g\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a proper lower-semicontinuous convex infimal convolution is attained at x through y and f is Gâteaux differentiable at y, then the infimal convolution is continuous and Gâteaux differentiable at x, with gradient equal to the gradient of f at y. Fréchet differentiability of f at y additionally yields Fréchet differentiability of the infimal convolution at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The statement is conditional on the product-space setup and coordinate maps R_i of Proposition 16.7.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gâteaux Differentiability and Singleton Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise characterization for proper convex functions on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper and convex, and let x\in\operatorname{dom}f. If f is G\^ateaux differentiable at x, then \partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}. Conversely, if x\in\operatorname{cont}f and \partial f(x)=\{u\}, then f is G\^ateaux differentiable at x and u=\nabla f(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, Gâteaux differentiability at a domain point makes the convex subdifferential the singleton containing the gradient. Conversely, at a continuity point, a singleton subdifferential implies Gâteaux differentiability and its unique element is the gradient.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ G\^ateaux differentiable at }x\Rightarrow\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\},\quad [x\in\operatorname{cont}f\text{ and }\partial f(x)=\{u\}]\Rightarrow[u=\nabla f(x)\text{ and }f\text{ is G\^ateaux differentiable at }x].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-to-Weak Continuity of the Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology-sensitive gradient regularity for Gâteaux-differentiable convex functions on Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) with \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function has nonempty domain interior and is Gâteaux differentiable throughout that interior, its gradient is continuous from the norm topology to the weak topology there.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gâteaux Differentiability via Strong-to-Weak Continuous Subgradient Selections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise equivalence at an interior domain point for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H) and x\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f. The following are equivalent: (i) f is G\^ateaux differentiable at x; (ii) every selection of \partial f is strong-to-weak continuous at x; (iii) at least one selection of \partial f is strong-to-weak continuous at x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function at an interior domain point, Gâteaux differentiability is equivalent both to strong-to-weak continuity there of every subdifferential selection and to the existence of one such continuous selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is G\^ateaux differentiable at }x\iff(\forall\text{ selections }s\text{ of }\partial f)\;s\text{ is strong-to-weak continuous at }x\iff(\exists\text{ a selection }s\text{ of }\partial f)\;s\text{ is strong-to-weak continuous at }x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary between convex subgradients and nonconvex generalized derivatives
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real normed space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition distinguishes the global convex-support subdifferential from local generalized derivatives used without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function lies in the convex regime when
\[f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\quad(\forall x,y\in X,\ \forall t\in[0,1]).\]
In this regime the convex subdifferential is
\[\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(x)=\{x^*\in X^*:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle x^*,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in X\}.\]
The convexity boundary is crossed when the displayed Jensen inequality fails for some \((x,y,t)\). Beyond that boundary, \(\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(x)\) still denotes global affine minorants if retained, but it is not a general local derivative: it may be empty at points of local interest and does not encode arbitrary local first-order behavior. A nonconvex statement must therefore name its replacement construction—such as a regular, limiting, or Clarke-type subdifferential—and its topology and regularity assumptions rather than silently reusing convex calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity means that every chord lies above the function. In that regime, a convex subgradient is a continuous affine global support. Crossing the boundary means that the convexity inequality fails somewhere. The same global-support set can still be written for a nonconvex function, but it is no longer a general local derivative and may be empty. Any extension must explicitly choose a generalized subdifferential and its assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper on a real normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of the Jensen inequality marks departure from the regime in which global supporting-affine subgradients furnish the canonical nonsmooth derivative.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For proper \(f\), convexity is equivalent to convexity of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable and convex at \(x\), then \(\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\) in a finite-dimensional or Hilbert identification.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex sum and chain rules cannot be transferred unchanged to an unspecified nonconvex generalized subdifferential.
boundary_notes: Different nonconvex subdifferentials are not interchangeable.
The inspected sources define convex subgradients but do not support a canonical choice among nonconvex generalized derivatives.

notation.meaning: Global convex-support subdifferential, explicitly distinguished from nonconvex constructions.

review_flags: A variational-analysis source is required for the named nonconvex generalized-subdifferential boundary.
No canonical nonconvex replacement was selected, preventing fabricated equivalences.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of a Global Affine Supporting Model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and fix \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). For \(v\in E\), identify \(v\) with the linear functional \(y\mapsto\langle v,y\rangle\), and define the affine model \(m_{\bar x,v}(y)=f(\bar x)+\langle v,y-\bar x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns exact global affine minorants touching the function at one point. It applies to arbitrary proper extended-real-valued functions in finite dimensions; convexity is not assumed, although convexity is the regime in which this construction becomes the standard convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in E\;\middle|\;f(y)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,y-\bar x\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in E\right\}.\] The function \(f\) has a global affine supporting model at \(\bar x\) precisely when \(\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\). It exhibits loss of global supporting models at \(\bar x\) precisely when \[\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)=\varnothing,\] equivalently, when for every \(v\in E\) there exists \(y\in E\) such that \(f(y)<f(\bar x)+\langle v,y-\bar x\rangle\). Function-level loss occurs when this condition holds at at least one point of \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper extended-real-valued function \(f\) and a finite point \(\bar x\), the global affine-support subdifferential consists of all slopes \(v\) whose affine model through \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) lies below \(f\) at every point. Global supporting models are lost at \(\bar x\) when this set is empty. Equivalently, every proposed slope is defeated somewhere by a point at which its affine model exceeds the function. The definition is pointwise: a nonconvex function may lose global support at some points while retaining it at others.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{loss at }\bar x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\forall v\in E)(\exists y\in E)\;f(y)<f(\bar x)+\langle v,y-\bar x\rangle.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[v\in\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m_{\bar x,v}\le f\ \text{on }E\ \text{and }m_{\bar x,v}(\bar x)=f(\bar x).\]
\[v\in\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in E}\bigl(f(y)-\langle v,y\rangle\bigr).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex, then \(\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\) is the usual convex subdifferential \(\partial f(\bar x)\).
For convex \(f\), \(v\in\partial f(\bar x)\) is equivalently characterized by \(\langle v,d\rangle\le f'(\bar x;d)\) for every direction \(d\in E\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \[0\in\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(y)\ge f(\bar x)\ \text{for all }y\in E,\] so a zero global subgradient characterizes a global minimizer even without convexity.
Whenever \(\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\), the epigraph of \(m_{\bar x,v}\) supplies a global one-sided affine model touching \(f\) at \(\bar x\).
boundary_notes: Nonconvexity alone does not imply \(\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)=\varnothing\) at every point; the loss condition must be checked at the specified point.
A local affine lower estimate with an error term is not a global supporting model. Such local objects belong to regular or limiting generalized-subdifferential theory.
The definition excludes \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\), where no finite touching affine model can be formed.

notation.meaning: Set of slopes of exact global affine minorants of the function that touch at the base point.
Affine model through the graph point \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) with slope \(v\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Monotone and Cyclically Monotone Potential Structure
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be a set-valued mapping with graph \(\operatorname{gph}T=\{(x,v)\mid v\in T(x)\}\). For a finite cycle, write \(x_{m+1}=x_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition isolates the graph property that distinguishes subdifferentials generated by proper closed convex potentials. Ordinary monotonicity is a two-point condition, while cyclic monotonicity tests cycles of arbitrary finite length and is the exact convex-potential condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(T\) is monotone when \[\langle x_1-x_0,v_1-v_0\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for all }(x_0,v_0),(x_1,v_1)\in\operatorname{gph}T.\] It is cyclically monotone when, for every integer \(m\ge1\) and every \((x_i,v_i)\in\operatorname{gph}T\), \[\sum_{i=0}^{m}\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,v_i\rangle\le0,\qquad x_{m+1}=x_0.\] The graph loses monotonicity if the two-point inequality is violated. It loses convex-potential structure if cyclic monotonicity is violated, namely if some finite cycle satisfies \[\sum_{i=0}^{m}\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,v_i\rangle>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping is monotone when every two graph points have a nonnegative displacement pairing. It is cyclically monotone when the sum of slope-displacement pairings around every finite closed cycle is nonpositive. Loss of monotonicity means that some pair violates the first condition. Loss of convex-potential structure means that some finite cycle violates the second condition. Cyclic monotonicity is the precise property permitting the graph to be contained in the subdifferential of a proper closed convex function; maximal cyclic monotonicity identifies graphs that are themselves such subdifferentials.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is a set-valued mapping.
For cyclic tests, \(m\ge1\) is arbitrary and \(x_{m+1}=x_0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[T\text{ is cyclically monotone}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists\text{ proper closed convex }f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ such that }T(x)\subseteq\partial f(x)\ \forall x.\]
\[T=\partial f\text{ for some proper closed convex }f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T\text{ is maximal cyclically monotone}.\]
The monotonicity inequality is the \(m=1\) instance of cyclic monotonicity.
special_cases_latex: For a proper convex function \(f\), its convex subdifferential \(\partial f\) is cyclically monotone and therefore monotone.
When \(n=1\), monotonicity and cyclic monotonicity coincide for these mappings; in dimensions \(n>1\), a mapping can be monotone without being cyclically monotone.

For a linear mapping \(T(x)=Qx\), cyclic monotonicity requires \(Q\) to be symmetric positive semidefinite, whereas monotonicity only requires the symmetric part \((Q+Q^*)/2\) to be positive semidefinite.
immediate_consequences_latex: Failure of ordinary monotonicity automatically implies failure of cyclic monotonicity.
If cyclic monotonicity fails, no proper closed convex function \(f\) can satisfy \(T(x)\subseteq\partial f(x)\) for every \(x\).
A graph may retain ordinary monotonicity yet lose its interpretation as a convex-potential subdifferential.
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert that every generalized subdifferential of every nonconvex function violates monotonicity; the graph inequalities must be tested for the chosen construction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-|x|\), the regular subgradient condition at \(0\) is \[\liminf_{x\to 0,\,x\ne 0}\frac{f(x)-f(0)-vx}{|x|}\geq 0.\] The one-sided limits make this impossible for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}\), so \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\). At each \(x\ne 0\), \(f\) is differentiable, with derivative \(-1\) for \(x>0\) and \(1\) for \(x<0\). Consequently, limits of nearby regular subgradients give \(\partial_L f(0)=\{-1,1\}\). Since \(f\) is locally Lipschitz, convexification gives the Clarke subdifferential \(\partial_C f(0)=\operatorname{co}\{-1,1\}=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After global convex support fails, regular, limiting, and Clarke subdifferentials can differ: for −|x| at zero they are empty, two-point, and interval-valued.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular subgradient is a vector whose affine model supports the function locally to first order, allowing an error negligible compared with distance from the base point. A limiting subgradient is a finite limit of regular subgradients taken at nearby points whose locations and function values both converge to those at the base point. A horizon subgradient records a limiting direction obtained by rescaling possibly unbounded nearby regular subgradients by positive scalars tending to zero. These local and sequential constructions remain meaningful for nonconvex extended-real-valued functions and replace the global-support interpretation used in convex analysis.
